subtopic: DELIVERY OF FOOD TO PERRY RIVER

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subtopic: DELIVERY OF FOOD TO PERRY RIVER
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, yesterday in the absence of the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources I sent him notice of a question. Perhaps he can answer it today. In view of the press reports that a Royal Canadian Air Force Dakota had been held up in its attempt to bring food to a number of starving Eskimos near Perry River, can the minister give the house any information as to whether that food has yet been delivered?

speakeroldname: Hon. Jean Lesage (Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources):
speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
subtopic: DELIVERY OF FOOD TO PERRY RIVER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker,
I wish to thank the hon. member for having

given me notice of his question. Perry River is an isolated community on the west of Queen Maud gulf. It is one of the more inaccessible parts of the Arctic area. It is on the mainland, but the closest R.C.M.P. post is at Cambridge Bay on Victoria island.
The report I received on Monday morning, January 25, stated that the caribou on which these people largely depend had moved out of that area during the winter, and that fish also had been comparatively scarce during the fall. The report further stated that some of the Eskimos had lost their dogs and had had to walk to the post in order to obtain food. The remaining dogs were in poor condition, and in order to save them dog feed was urgently required.
It will be noted from what I have just said that no Eskimos were starving, as the hon. member has just said in his question. Dogs, huskies, were starving. This was on Monday last, January 25, and it was the first intimation the department in Ottawa had about this situation.
The trading post at Perry River is operated by an Eskimo named Angulalik, who has a radio receiver but no transmitter. The area is patrolled twice a year by the R.C.M.P. detachment at Cambridge Bay, and it was while on his regular semi-annual patrol that Constable Ferguson became aware of this situation. Ordinarily he would have advised headquarters of "G" division of the R.C.M.P. here in Ottawa. However, in view of the urgency the constable apparently radioed the subdivision headquarters at Fort Smith. The inspector there immediately conferred with our district administrator at Fort Smith, and together they arranged with the R.C.A.F. command headquarters at Edmonton to make a plane available to take relief supplies immediately to Perry River. As a result, 2,400 pounds of buffalo meat from the buffalo slaughter at Wood Buffalo park have been sent.
As a matter of fact the R.C.A.F. plane tried to land at Perry River on Monday morning, the 25th, but could not locate the settlement. It will be realized that at this time of the year, with the exception of a few hours of twilight in the morning, it is pitch dark in the Arctic. A radio message was then broadcast on Monday last to Angulalik, asking him to light flares on the following morning. But then the plane was kept to the ground at Yellowknife because of bad weather. It was later on Tuesday that the plane could fly to Cambridge Bay, where it waited for the weather to clear, and landed later on the 27th, at Perry River, with supplies, which it unloaded.
Inquiries of the Ministry
I believe that one has to be very careful with sweeping conclusions with respect to starving Eskimos. I am informed that both the Royal Canadian Mounted Police and officers of the Department of Northern Affairs and National Resources are doing the very difficult job of patrolling these barren lands for thousands of miles. I am informed that there has been no Eskimo who has starved. A few huskies have starved, but the Eskimos went to the post of Angulalik and were fed; and as soon as we were made aware of the situation a plane was flown in with the necessary supplies for the huskies. It might be, of course, that the hon. member for Saskatoon (Mr. Knight) has got something from Farley Mowat's book. Maybe the sweeping conclusions in the book, based upon false information, are contagious.
And, by the way, I have looked into the matter of Farley Mowat's book, which was mentioned the other day by the hon. member.
I have looked at the book and I have had some of the affirmations of Mr. Mowat checked. I have no time to recount everything that is said in the book, but I think that one of the stories is worth mentioning here. Mr. Mowat says at one point that there was slaughter of caribou-

maintopic: MEASURES TO PROTECT DAIRY INDUSTRY AGAINST OVERPRODUCTION

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

maintopic: MEASURES TO PROTECT DAIRY INDUSTRY AGAINST OVERPRODUCTION
speechtext: I should like to direct a question to the Minister of Agriculture. Is he aware of representations made by the Quebec farmers' associations, and particularly by the dairy farmers' association of Canada, concerning the overproduction of butter this year? If so, are measures to be taken to protect the dairy industry?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Gardiner (Minister of Agriculture):
maintopic: MEASURES TO PROTECT DAIRY INDUSTRY AGAINST OVERPRODUCTION
speechtext:
I wish to thank the hon. member for having given me a copy of his question yesterday, which gave me an opportunity of checking in the department with regard to the statements which are made.
The first part of the question asked whether I was aware of representations made by the Quebec farmers' associations. My answer to that, of course, would be yes. I have had some of these representations made to me directly, and particularly by the dairy farmers' association of Canada. I have read the discussions which took place in Hamilton, and those which took place in London recently with regard to the matter. The question then goes on and says, "concerning the overproduction of butter this year", and then asks whether some measures are to be taken to protect the dairy industry. In answer to that I would say that we took the actions that we thought were necessary six years ago when we set up the system under which butter is handled in Canada at the present time.
We had in mind at that time two objectives. The first was to maintain a reasonable return to producers in the summer months. Hon. members will recall that prior to that time there was a margin of 10 cents to 12 cents a pound on butter as between the price paid in the summertime and the price at which it was sold in the winter. Therefore we took the action we did six years ago in order to overcome that difficulty; and, in the second place, to assure a reasonable cost to consumers in the winter months.
The present position is that a story is being circulated that we shall have 43 million pounds of butter on May 1 next. Well, our records do not indicate that. Our records indicate that we may have around 30 million pounds, and that is not an amount which would give any difficulties to those who are handling butter in this country, the reason 

being there are about 1 million people more in the country now eating butter than there were a few years ago. Therefore the amount of butter which has to be in the pipe line in order to assure distribution is somewhat greater than it was at that time.
It was then rated at about 10 million pounds. It is now found that with the wider distribution of settlement it takes something over 12 million pounds in order to keep the pipe line supplied, so that even 30 million pounds of butter is not an amount which would create any great difficulty. The chief reason why it is up 5 million or 6 million pounds above last year is that we were not able to sell any dairy cows in the United States during 1952, and the fact that those dairy cows were still here in 1953 brought about a greater production of milk, and therefore a greater production of butter last year than we otherwise would have had. But at the present time not only are we again selling dairy cows in the United States, but in 1953 we sold 40,000. In the four years before 1952 we sold 47,000, so that last year we were only 7,000 below the four years preceding 1952.
That sale of 40,000 cows into the United States has been supplemented by a very large sale of female stock for slaughter in this country during recent months, so that from now down until the end of the year we do not expect that the production will be so great as to cause any great difficulty here. We require at least 25 million pounds of butter in this country on May 1 in order to make sure that the consumer in Canada is going to be served with butter at a price which is not out of line in the winter months. In order to assure hon. members that that is true this year, butter has sold all this winter at a cent a pound wholesale lower than it did last year. It is selling this year at 61 cents a pound; it sold last year at 62 cents. This is because we have enough butter to supply the trade adequately until May 1.
Therefore the objectives which we have in mind, one, of assuring the farmer a payment on the basis of 58 cents a pound throughout the whole year, and the other of assuring the consumer that in the costly months of the winter he does not have to pay on a basis higher than 61 cents, are being achieved, and we do not think there is any necessity for changing the policy at the present time in any way whatsoever. We think it is succeeding. It has succeeded in the interests of both the producer and the consumer.

speechtext:
On January 28 the hon.

We have no specific information on this particular ordinance but we have received general reports on the state of foreign business in communist China. From these reports it would appear that the Peking government is moving in a direction which will make the continued operation of many foreign business concerns in mainland China so difficult that they would be compelled to withdraw. This is not surprising because western residents and western interests have been progressively ousted by the communist regime since it came to power four years ago.
The ordinance to which the hon. member referred would appear to be a local implementation in Tientsin of this general policy of the communist government.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS TO INCREASE SALARIES OF SPEAKERS AND DEPUTY SPEAKER, SESSIONAL ALLOWANCES OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when the debate w;as adjourned last night I had pointed out certain reasons why I supported the increase in the sessional indemnity of members of parliament proposed in this bill. I had pointed out that in my opinion such increase was in the best interests of parliament itself. I had pointed out that in my opinion it was in the best interests of good government in this country that the House of Commons should be representative of a broad cross-section of the Canadian public.
I had pointed out that with the length of our parliamentary sessions running from six to eight months and the additional time required for work in and on behalf of our constituencies very little time was left for any hon. member to devote to his private business or profession. Furthermore I had pointed out that in my opinion it was not in the interests of good government that members of this house should be forced by economic necessity to neglect the business of this house, to shorten its sessions or to limit the number of those sessions because of the necessity of attending to their private business or profession.
Furthermore, I had pointed out that if we are to get representation from trade unions, from workers and from certain professions, those representatives must accept this as a full-time job. There just is no opportunity for certain classes of people who come here for six or eight months in the year as members of parliament to go back and participate in their former jobs or occupations.

Senate and House of Commons
The question comes up of course as to just what is an equitable or fair increase. I have no doubt whatever that we could find in this country 265 representatives who would come here even for $4,000. I think probably we could get 265 members to come here for as little as $3,000 if we set that as the limit. I think we could easily get 265 representatives across Canada who had never earned $3,000 a year in their lives and who would be glad to come here. But I do not think that that would make a good House of Commons.
On the other hand, I am quite confident that we could get 265 members to come here who had reached the age or degree of economic security where they were no longer dependent in any way upon the amount of sessional indemnity that would be paid. They could come here financially independent. But I do not think that that would make for a good representative parliament.
If we are to draw from a broad crosssection of the Canadian public, if we are to draw from all ranks of the Canadian public men and women who have demonstrated their abilities in their own chosen fields, then in my opinion we must be prepared to pay an indemnity that will relieve them of financial worry, that will leave them free to spend whatever time is required by public business in this house, and to devote their time and energies to the interests of their constituencies.
There are in the chamber those who have indicated that they consider the $10,000 figure too high and would like to settle for $8,000. I indicated last night that in my opinion the $10,000 indemnity is not too high. It is not out of line with the salaries that the Canadian taxpayer and Canadian consumer are paying to men and women holding positions of comparable responsibilities. I gave one example. We have only to look over the field of executives and managers in business and industry and compare their responsibilities with those of members of parliament to discover that commerce and industry pay their executives salaries of $10,000 and more.
What we are sometimes apt to forget is that every dollar paid to managers and directors of industry and commerce is paid by the Canadian consumer just as truly as if those dollars were collected in taxes. There are some of us who are inclined to differentiate between money paid to managers and directors of private enterprise and that which is paid to managers and directors and representatives of publicly-owned industries and institutions. It is the Canadian consumer who in the final analysis pays those salaries to private enterprise just as truly as it is

the Canadian taxpayer and consumer who pays the indemnities of members of parliament.
The province of Ontario now pays the members of its legislative assembly $4,000 for a six-weeks session. I have heard no great uproar of public opinion in Ontario against that indemnity. If members of the Ontario legislature require $4,000 for a six-weeks session, then I submit there is every reason to believe that we in this house with a six or eight months session are entitled to at least $10,000.
Objection has been raised that the $10,000 indemnity is going to separate us from the great mass of people whom we represent. The suggestion is made that because the income level of the majority of Canadian people is below the income level that we would be in, we would thus be separated from our constituents. In my opinion the amount of income received by the individual representative is not a main or major factor in separating him from his constituents. If the people of Canada had wanted to send to Ottawa at the last general election members who came within their own income group, that is in the $2,000, $3,000 or $4,000 bracket, they had ample opportunity to do so. In nearly every constituency across this country there were C.C.F. candidates standing for office who were in the same low income bracket as the majority of those whom they sought to represent.
The Canadian public gave no demonstration of their desire to send to parliament the representatives who belonged to their own income group. I have had some experience with the Canadian voter and I have found the voter is much more interested in voting for someone who has made good in his own profession or business and who has raised himself above the general economic level of the people he is seeking to represent than he is in sending someone who belongs entirely to his own income group. I believe the idea that $10,000 in indemnities is going to cut us off from association with, interest in, or sympathy for our constituents is fear and nothing more than fear.
We have heard a great deal about the needs of old age pension recipients and those in receipt of veterans allowances, and how we should first attend to them. I hear from a great many people on old age pensions. As a matter of fact, I went through my files last night and I found something in the neighbourhood of 50 letters from old age pensioners in my own riding, all of which were written since my arrival back here on January 12.

Most of these 50 letters from old age pensioners have been addressed to me since this subject we are now discussing became publicized in our newspapers. In not one single instance has any one of them indicated in any shape or form that he considered it would be reprehensible for me to accept an increase in my indemnity until I had secured an increase in their old age pension. They asked for an increase in their pensions; they pointed out their need; but not one has suggested that my acceptance of an increase in my indemnity is going to deprive them of any increase in their pension.
If the government feel they could not increase old age pensions because they are called upon to give members of parliament and the Senate an increase in their indemnities, but could do so were such members to forgo that increase, I do not think there is a member in this house who would object to forgoing this increase until the old age pension was increased. The fact is, there is very little relation between the proposed increases in indemnities and the amount paid to old age pensioners.
Much more could be done for old age pensioners by the provincial governments of the provinces in which they live, if these governments were so inclined to consider it.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS TO INCREASE SALARIES OF SPEAKERS AND DEPUTY SPEAKER, SESSIONAL ALLOWANCES OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS TO INCREASE SALARIES OF SPEAKERS AND DEPUTY SPEAKER, SESSIONAL ALLOWANCES OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext:
As a matter of fact, I am delighted to find that the government considers there are no difficulties in the way of providing us with these increases, and that there is sufficient income in the treasury for that purpose. I am sure the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) would not sanction these increases for cabinet ministers, members of parliament and the Senate if he did not feel there was going to be something in the treasury for our old age pensioners and those in receipt of veterans allowances. If I thought for one moment that the acceptance of this increased indemnity would delay an increase in old age pensions or veterans allowances I would forgo that increase, and I am confident every member in this house would be willing to do the same.
Certainly, there is a crying need for increases in old age pensions and veterans allowances. One of the ways to achieve that increase is to send to this parliament men and women who will show a greater interest in these older citizens and veterans. I do not think they will get that opportunity simply by keeping us on an economic level where year in, year out, we have to borrow and go into debt in order to remain here. That, Mr. Speaker, has been my experience every year since I first came to Ottawa in 1942.
Senate and House of Commons

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS TO INCREASE SALARIES OF SPEAKERS AND DEPUTY SPEAKER, SESSIONAL ALLOWANCES OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, at the resolution stage of this debate I spoke, as usual, without notes and I omitted some matters which I had intended to mention with respect to members of the other place.
Our constitutional system provides for an upper and lower house, and as long as we continue to conduct the nation's affairs in that manner members of the upper house should not be, I believe, on a lower plane than members of the House of Commons. The official opposition has intimated that they do not wish to abolish the Senate. But what do they intend that we should do? Do they want to starve members of the upper house and force them out of the positions as public servants, or are they prepared to offer some constructive measure whereby these members can remain on a level similar to that of members of the House of Commons?
I do not want to be a member of this house and yet feel that I can look upon the members of the upper house with perhaps less respect than I would accord to our protective staff in this chamber. That will be the result if we do not determine that we are going to maintain a proper balance without discrimination.
There are perhaps a few matters which should be brought to the attention of the house at this time with respect to this question of increases in indemnities for members of parliament. As I said the other day, the hon. member for Simcoe North (Mr. Ferguson) was the first member of parliament in my time to broach this question of the inadequacies of the rates of pay and conditions under which members live here in Ottawa. This makes me reflect for a moment. Taking note of the debate in this house, may I say that if I were again in the position of choosing a bargaining committee I certainly would know where to go in this house; it would be to those people who believe that a man is worthy of his hire.
The hon. member for Simcoe North, speaking in the debate on May 1, 1952, had some extremely interesting comments to make relative to this matter.

speechtext:
It is 1952. Certainly the
quotation is relevant. The date of the debate
16S4	HOUSE OF
Senate and House of Commons is May 1, 1952. I quote from the speech of the hon. member for Simcoe North as reported at page 1774 of Hansard of that year:
What can the people of Canada expect when their representatives, who are supposed to hold one of the highest offices in Canada, are shown the lack of consideration which they are receiving from this government.
He was speaking, of course, of the government in power. Then again:
Let me say this to the members of the House of Commons. If the people of Canada want in parliament the men they need, $4,000 a year or a session is far too little to attract such men. It is far too little to bring into parliament the type of men the people of Canada need.
May I say that if ever a party needed a shot in the arm, it is the one to which the hon. member belongs. Again I quote:
The labour unions of this country would consider it an insult to offer their leaders the stipend which is offered to the makers of the laws of this country, the men who appoint the judiciary of this country, namely $4,000 a year with $2,000 expenses.
He continues:
I do not know of a member of parliament who does not know, when he comes here at that remuneration, that he is compelled to live in a room on the third floor of a rooming house in Ottawa.
A day or two ago, in my speech I said that a member should not be expected to live in a garret when he was in Ottawa representing his constituency. I said that I spoke without notes the other evening, but one would almost imagine that I was reading from the speech made by the hon. member for Simcoe North, whose party at this point does not seem to be anxious to make the suggestions that he then saw fit to make. I quote further from his speech:
He cannot afford to live in proper quarters such as the Chateau Laurier unless he takes the money from his own pocket.
I now quote further from the speech; there is here also a relevant matter, Mr. Speaker, that I am leaving out, as it is not as outstanding as are these portions which I choose to quote. I quote again:
If he is the right kind of man he knows of these responsibilities when he offers himself for election. But the members of this government, which has the people of Canada under its thumb, in the length of time they have sat in office have not been men enough to come forward and raise the salaries of the representatives of the people to an amount which is somewhere near what it ought to be.
And this is the crowning statement:
It is a disgraceful situation.
It is infamous, I would say. I quote further:
How can we conscientiously feel that we, as a body, are responsible for appointing judges at $8,000 a year, how can we feel responsible for the making of the laws to be administered by those judges, at this disgraceful and insulting remuneration of $4,000 a year?


If it is that bad, it is worthy of a 100 per cent increase, in my estimation. I quote again:
Surely you are not afraid to stand on your feet and tell your constituents that you believe you are worth greater compensation for your efforts.
I pause here for a moment, Mr. Speaker, to point out that some hon. members have been called to order because they have inferred that the position taken by some of the members may have a political bias. I therefore go on to prove that the hon. member for Simcoe North had that feeling himself. He said:
If the people do not think so, at election time they will tell you so, me included. Most of the members feel as I do, but they sit back and say, "I don't think it is good politics to mention that."
But the hon. member goes on further to say:
I am not built that way. I am sent here to mention matters which I believe are of vital importance to the people of Canada, whether it means my defeat or my re-election. At the end of my term the voters will decide.
When making their estimates of the debate and of the manner in which we vote on this question, I hope the voters will decide as the hon. member for Simcoe North suggested they should.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS TO INCREASE SALARIES OF SPEAKERS AND DEPUTY SPEAKER, SESSIONAL ALLOWANCES OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I appreciated the last remarks of the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) when he was introducing the resolution foreshadowing this bill,

wherein he said it would be up to each member of parliament, himself or herself, to decide whether to support the resolution or to support the bills that would follow, based on the resolution.
During the last year, both in the election campaign and since then, I have endeavoured to be honest with my constituents and with myself in discussing this particular subject. I said then-and I repeat it now-that as far as I was concerned, if the indemnity was to be placed on an annual basis, there would have to be some revision upwards. I said to them-and I repeat it now-that as far as I was concerned the income of members of parliament was quite satisfactory in the last four years but that if the basis upon which that indemnity is paid should be changed and if, as a result of that change, the indemnity should drop, I for one would feel that the result would not provide an indemnity sufficient to enable the average member of parliament to give his best service to his constituents.
When the leader of this group moves in committee that the $8,000 indemnity figure be reduced to $6,000, thus making the total $8,000 instead of $10,000-I shall be pleased to support that amendment. I cannot support second reading of this bill since it provides a total pay of $10,000 to members of the other place. I believe those hon. gentlemen in the other place are receiving now a reasonable remuneration in keeping with the services they render to the people of Canada.
I should like to see a further provision dealing with absenteeism which would make it impossible for any member of the house, even though no member of the house might do it, to be absent from this house for all of a session and still collect a large part of the pay involved. I have heard speeches for this bill and against it. I doubt if there are many in this house who really believe that the pay members of parliament have received over the last four years has been too much. My opposition to this bill is based, therefore, on the provision that the pay of members shall be increased over what it has been. I do not think that is necessary. I do not think it is desirable.
A great many speeches have been made during this debate to the effect that members of parliament must have a sufficient income in order to faithfully discharge their many duties, and that the remuneration of members must be sufficient to attract outstanding men to the house. I believe that the income members have received over the last four years has been sufficient to accomplish all
Senate and House of Commons of these desired objectives. When I look around the house I find that there are many extremely able members, and so far as I am concerned none of them has been attracted here because of the pay. I believe, rather, they have been attracted here because they believe that by coming here they can provide a service to the people of Canada. I believe that if changes were made in this bill now to provide for members in the next four years the same pay as they received during the last four years, such a bill would pass unanimously or with very few dissenting votes.
I believe the pay members have received has been sufficient in recent years. The Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) stated that the problem with which we are dealing, wherein members have to come to Ottawa for long periods and have not too much time to spend in their regular professions, must be dealt with in two ways. The first way, he said, would be by shortening the length of the sessions, and the second way by increasing the sessional indemnity of members to $8,000. I say that if we are successful in reducing the length of the sessions- and I believe that is what the committee which has been set up will likely accomplish-then an increase to $10,000 becomes that much less necessary. I have worked out on a monthly basis what $10,000 will mean. Of course the whole sum is not to be paid on a monthly basis but for the purpose of this calculation I have assumed that it is. A married man would then receive $713 per month after having paid all his income taxes and his deductions to the pension fund. I believe that $713 per month is a very large sum of money, an unnecessarily large sum of money.
On the other hand, if the indemnity were made $6,000, along with the expense allowance of $2,000, for a married man that would work out at $583 per month after income tax and pension fund deductions. Speaking for myself, I believe members of parliament can get along on approximately $583 per month, as in recent years. I believe they could provide reasonable and suitable housing accommodation for their families in Ottawa, then could go back to their constituents for the remaining six months and perform a reasonable job for their constituents. I feel that $10,000 total pay for members is unnecessary. It has been said by some that if you put members in the $10,000 category, they will begin to think differently and they may lose, at least to some extent, contact with

Senate and House of Commons their constituents. It is said that will condition their thinking and make them look at problems in a different light.
This may or may not be true. I rather doubt that it would change the opinion or attitude of most members of parliament. I do believe, however, that if you pay members a very high salary you will change the attitude of the electors to their representatives. The people whom the member represents will believe that there is such a disparity between incomes, they will feel far removed from their representative, and that will make it more difficult for the member to perform the functions of a representative.
The Prime Minister pointed out that the sessional indemnity has not been altered since 1920. He went on to say that rising costs since that time made an upward adjustment necessary, and this is the upward adjustment the government felt was necessary. If you look at the cost of living back in 1920, you will find the consumer price index for Canada stood at 90-5; for 1953 the cost of living index stood at 116. In other words, there has been a 29 per cent increase in the cost of living since 1920, when the last increase in the sessional indemnity took place. I honestly feel that a 100 per cent increase in the indemnity at this time is too much. When I consider that there is a $2,000 tax-free allowance included in the $10,000, which means an increase of 150 per cent over 1920, 1 feel that the provisions of this bill are not at all necessary.
I naturally think of the position of my constituents in the agricultural industry. I have calculated the index for farm products in 1920 at 254; that was the level of farm prices. During 1953, and today, the level of farm prices has been well under that of 1920. According to the official statistics of the dominion bureau of statistics, the agricultural industry is in a worse position now than it was in 1920, yet members of parliament are to be put in a much better position by a 150 per cent increase in their remuneration.
As I have said, I believe the pay members of parliament have been receiving for the last few years is sufficient. Members would on that basis receive $583 a month take-home pay. The Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) has said an effort will be made to shorten hours, and that would make the burden of members of parliament somewhat less. And if a representative in the House of Commons is elected three times, he can retire then at the end of eight years on a pension of $120 a month for life. Not all members will qualify for pension. But if after having received $583 a month, on the


basis of our income for the last four years, a member is defeated in an election, he will have a nest egg in the pension fund which will permit him to withdraw $960. If he is here for two parliaments and is then defeated, that nest egg will amount to $1,920.
I submit that if the pay of members of parliament is to be placed on an annual basis it should be on a basis which will not reduce the income of those members as compared with the level in the last preceding parliament.
I hope the government will reconsider the measure, and will take steps to reduce the amount of the indemnity in line with the suggestion made by the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell).

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS TO INCREASE SALARIES OF SPEAKERS AND DEPUTY SPEAKER, SESSIONAL ALLOWANCES OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a question of privilege. The hon. member for Notre Dame de Grace (Mr. Hamilton) said that I made an erroneous statement yesterday concerning him. I must say that the hon. member has not taken much trouble to read what I said at that time with respect to the councillors in the city of Montreal.
What I said yesterday appears at page 1662 of Hansard, and it is in these words:
All three different classes of councillors are given the same treatment. However, the class C councillors are not elected by the people, but are named to council by their own organizations. In the class C group, if one is a member of the executive committee he will receive $7,000 a year, just the same as any other member of the executive who must be elected. Indeed, we find that the hon. member for Notre Dame de Grace (Mr. Hamilton) is in class C, in the city of Montreal; and as such he is paid the same amount that is paid to the members who are elected by the people.
As anyone can see, I never said that the hon. member for Notre Dame de Grace was a member of the Montreal city executive, and hence receiving $7,000 a year. I note that the hon. member is not a member of the city executive in Montreal, and I never said the contrary. I know also that his pay is $1,500 per annum and no more. I hope that in future the hon. member for Notre Dame de Grace will read my remarks in this chamber more carefully, and avoid rising on questions of privilege when there is no ground for that procedure.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS TO INCREASE SALARIES OF SPEAKERS AND DEPUTY SPEAKER, SESSIONAL ALLOWANCES OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, yesterday while speaking to Bill No. 171 the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Low), leader of the Social Credit group, made two or three statements to which I think I should make reference at this time.
In the first place he stressed the fact that it was his conviction this issue is not one of

a party character. Certainly I agree with that. I think it should be considered in any other sense but a party sense. He stressed the fact also that the issue is one upon which every member should take his own stand. I agree absolutely; and I trust that when the vote is called each and every member of the House of Commons will stay in the house and take his stand. I trust we shall not have to witness a rush of humans to the lobbies.
Certainly I am fully prepared to take my stand. I listened with a great deal of interest to the observations of the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Argue). I was rather surprised to hear him use the expression "take-home pay" in such a loose fashion. After all, his party claims to have the ear of labour. Certainly no member of a labour organization would make the declaration that a member of parliament would have take-home pay of $583 a month. Certainly my hon. friend took into account the income tax, and he took into account the deductions under the members' retirement plan. But certainly he gave every evidence of having ignored such things as driving one's automobile 15,000 or 20,000 miles every year, and not being able to allow depreciation, or one cent of cost of operation, when filing income tax returns.
Certainly, he did not take into consideration the cost of remaining in Ottawa for as many as eight or nine months in a given year-and some of us have done this for the past fourteen years. Certainly he did not take into account at the same time the cost of maintaining a home and one's family elsewhere. Certainly, sir, there were a number of other things, too, which were not taken into account.
I challenge the statement that there has been any such sum, or any sum even remotely resembling $583 a month. Some of us have been here for quite some time. Although I have been a member for only fourteen years, I believe this is my nineteenth session of parliament; and I have had sufficient experience during that time to talk with some slight degree of authority.
Secondly, I find myself exasperated when I pick up newspaper after newspaper and see reference made to a proposed indemnity of $10,000. Certainly it is not that, and it will not be that, even if this bill is given approval. It is an indemnity of $8,000. As all members know, we are not allowed to make any deductions because of being away from home when, necessarily, we are away. We cannot make deductions on that account, as do the railwaymen and many other groups
Senate and House of Commons of employees. My understanding is that the $2,000 is to compensate in part-and it compensates only in part-for our being away during those weeks and months, not only during sessions of parliament but during the twelve months of the year.
I become exasperated when I read, too, the inferences left for the public to draw, that once a session of parliament is prorogued the members have finished their work until the next session begins. Anyone who has done his duty as a member, and certainly anyone who has had experience in parliament, realizes the fallaciousness of that argument.
This position is becoming more and more demanding all the time. Not only is it more demanding on one's time, but it is also more demanding on one's finances. And when one leaves this House of Commons at the end of a session it is to just take up another phase of his work, which costs him money, which requires a great deal of time and involves, I would go so far as to say, innumerable headaches.
While the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Low) made it perfectly clear that he was expressing his own views, I can assure him that he expressed mine, and I can also assure him that it is my conviction he expressed the views of the majority of the members of this House of Commons. I have listened with a good deal of interest to the arguments which have been advanced in opposition to Bill No. 171. I can do no other than characterize a good number of those arguments as being utterly fantastic.
It annoys me, Mr. Speaker, no end to have some hon. members create the impression- I do not know whether it is by design or otherwise; I am probably not competent to judge-that the passage of this bill will take something away from old age pensioners, or that it will take something away from our war veterans. That is utter nonsense. Not only is it untrue that it takes something away, but it is equally untrue that it would prevent them from securing more in the days to come.
Last week the hon. member for Macleod (Mr. Hansell) made it abundantly clear that if he felt that by supporting this measure it would prevent our securing more for our old age pensioners or for our war veterans allowance recipients, then he would oppose it. Well, I am sure that we would all oppose it. In this connection I was rather surprised to see an extract or two from the Vancouver Province. On January 28, on the front page

Senate and House of Commons of the Vancouver Province, under the heading "C.C.F. plans battle on old age pensions", it stated:
Several members referred to pensioners during the debate on parliamentary indemnities, but took the attitude, directly or indirectly, that whether or not M.P.'s salaries were increased it would be economically impossible to boost pensions.
E. G. Hansell (Social Credit, Macleod) for instance, said he was sure that if it were a question of raising M.P.'s salaries or pensions that "every hon. member would say, by all means increase the old age pensions and war veterans' allowances."
Yet on the editorial page of that same issue, Mr. Speaker, reference is made to the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway (Mr. Maclnnis) and he is quoted in this way:
He would not support any increase-
Incidentally, this is not a verbatim quotation; only part of it is verbatim. I continue:
He would not support any increase until parliament "made some attempt at raising the incomes of the poor people of this rich country."
Here is what the editorial goes on to say:
He was the one member who spoke up for the old age pensioners.
How an editor of a paper could write such an editorial in the light of the news item which appeared on the front page of the same issue is more than I can understand. I criticize and condemn any attempt on the part of any newspaper to try to create the impression that there are certain members in this House of Commons who would take an increase in indemnity, knowing that our pensioners and our war veterans would suffer as a consequence.
As I say, I condemn any attempt of that kind. I repeat my conviction, and I think it is the conviction of most of us here, that adequate compensation to members of the House of Commons takes nothing away from these people or from other people whom I have mentioned. It will not lessen in any sense whatsoever our will and our determination to press for more adequate compensation for those groups of people. In fact, this could easily provide means for more concerted pressure on behalf of those people. If this argument that has been advanced, this argument that I have condemned, has any merit, then we would not be justified as a House of Commons in making any move whatever on behalf of any group of people in this country until we were prepared to act similarly on behalf of all people countrywide. We would not be justified under any guaranteed floor price set-up to pay any producer of this country a cent more than he is getting simply because, if what is said is true, it would be most unfair to all other groups within the country. It is a fantastic argument.

I was amazed also to hear it said in this house that adequate compensation for members of parliament would separate us from the people whom we represent. Whoever makes a declaration of that kind is the very one who would say, if put under pressure: "It will separate you, but it will not separate me." I believe under pressure that is what would be said. I am amazed that any hon. member in this house would state that adequate compensation could offer the least threat of separating him from his people. I am amazed also at the suggestion that that hon. member's relationship with his constituency is governed by dollars and cents. I would suggest that such a declaration does in effect condemn all those members of parliament who had, when they came into this house, means which might have set them economically above some of the people in the country; but I would not be a party to any such condemnation, because I have known members of parliament of this house too well and too long to make any such assertion.
If any member of parliament, by virtue of the fact that he receives adequate compensation, is separated from his constituents as a consequence thereof, then I am certain that when the next election comes along the electors will take care of him. I doubt whether it is a matter that we should concern ourselves with. It has no validity in fact.
I have heard references to letters, Mr. Speaker. One would almost conclude that half a dozen letters represents the general opinion of probably 50,000 people in a constituency or 14 million people across this country. Probably I am as close to the people whom I represent as are other hon. members. I have not received a single solitary letter condemning members of parliament for accepting this contemplated increase, not one single solitary letter, and I know there are over 50,000 people in my constituency. In fact, the only references that have been made to it have been made just as an aside in another letter, and in every case they have expressed gratification that we were going to be adequately compensated, Mr. Speaker.
I am one of those persons who have never hesitated to keep their electors informed with respect to their financial problems, and probably because of the fact that I have kept them informed they see this thing in the light in which it should be seen. In glancing at newspaper editorials I have noticed general agreement with the idea of adequately compensated members of parliament. In fact I have seen the figure of $10,000 at the head of more than one editorial.

One or two ideas have been expressed. One was relative to the other house and others were relative to the $2,000 tax-free allowance. However, by and large the newspaper editorials have supported the type of compensation for members of parliament envisaged in the bill now before us. In fact, I am absolutely convinced that it meets with the approval of the majority of the people from coast to coast.
Someone referred to a Gallup poll. If I could take a Gallup poll and make sure that I "galluped" the right people I could probably get a majority of them to agree that the indemnity should be cut by 50 per cent. I do not put too much stock in that kind of so-called evidence.
I have no desire to take up too much time but I was interested in some of the observations of the hon. member for York South (Mr. Noseworthy). It so happens that he and I were members of the same profession. It also happens that this is one of those cases where when you are chosen as a member of parliament you must give up the work you are doing. How in the world could one carry on as a school teacher when the house from time to time is in session from September to December and from late January until June? It would be utterly fantastic.
It is not up to this House of Commons to say whether I should or should not devote all my time to my work as a member of parliament. That is up to the electors in my constituency to decide. During each of the last four elections I have told them that there was one thing they could be certain of: that if I were elected I intended to devote my full time to what I considered to be a full-time job. They made their decision as to whether I should be their member of parliament or whether somebody else should be their member. I am not saying that they made their decision entirely on that basis, but certainly they have come to realize that it is a twelvemonth job. Even if someone is in another type of profession or occupation or business and is able to carry on, the fact is that some of them certainly have not been able to do so completely. In fact, some have been ruined as a consequence of having served as members of parliament. They have been ruined as far as their private businesses are concerned. It is too much of a sacrifice even for those who are desirous of making sacrifices to be called upon to make.
I have heard a great deal of reference to this figure of $8,000 as an indemnity. I agree with the hon. member for Peace River and am absolutely confident that the government and the treasury board did not say "eeny, 83276-107
Senate and House of Commons meeny, miny, mo" and pick a figure out of some hat. They must have given long and earnest consideration to this. It is the easiest thing in the world to say that $8,000 is too much and that $6,000 is enough. It is easy enough to say a good many of the things that have been said here, but I do not intend to be swayed too much by that kind of argument.
I am confident that the people I represent desire that a job should be done by their member. They are willing to pay what is required in order that that job might be done in the way they want it done. I have no hesitation whatsoever in saying to this House of Commons that the proposal contained in this bill represents nothing more than what to me appears adequate at this time under current conditions. We do not live in anything but a moderate fashion.
I say without hesitation that it is most difficult for a member of parliament who is called upon to do certain things on behalf of the people he represents to find that he must curtail his activities on their behalf because he simply has not the money to do it or because he realizes that he would have to go into debt to do it. I would have no hesitation in opening my financial accounts to the membership of this house after having been a member for fourteen years. I am not ashamed of them, because I think they would be a reflection of the conditions which have faced a good many members of this house.
I notice that it is not only here that these matters are being considered. Provincial governments have considered this matter from time to time and have made adjustments in the indemnities payable to their members. It has already been pointed out that in one province at least they receive more than we do now in the way of actual indemnity and that in the province in which we find ourselves now they receive an equal amount.
I am not complaining about that, but I do contend that there is something wrong in the relationship that exists between the two. For example, I find that in some provinces they are considering paying pensions to their cabinet ministers. I am not criticizing that. I have a Canadian Press clipping here which appeared in a local paper on Saturday which states:
A plan to provide pensions to Saskatchewan cabinet members may be considered by the government before the legislature opens February 11, it was reported Friday. Only one provincial government, Nova Scotia, now has a pension plan for cabinet members.
I am not criticizing that; in fact I would be the first one to say that when a man has

Senate and House of Commons served in a provincial cabinet for a period of years, when he gives his full time to that service, he should receive a pension. I simply remind the house that these matters are being considered, even pensions for cabinet ministers, by certain provinces, Saskatchewan in particular. I do not refer to this in any critical way because I believe it should be done in every province across Canada.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS TO INCREASE SALARIES OF SPEAKERS AND DEPUTY SPEAKER, SESSIONAL ALLOWANCES OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext: I agree with that.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS TO INCREASE SALARIES OF SPEAKERS AND DEPUTY SPEAKER, SESSIONAL ALLOWANCES OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext: Having said that, perhaps I have said enough. I think I have given the house a pretty clear picture of where I stand. I have not asked my colleagues, but I think if I took a vote right now I would have them with me on this matter.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS TO INCREASE SALARIES OF SPEAKERS AND DEPUTY SPEAKER, SESSIONAL ALLOWANCES OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to put my position briefly on the record. I believe the house should feel indebted to the hon. member who has just spoken for answering the rather specious argument which has been made with regard to the $583 take-home pay by the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Argue). If I had not had any previous experience about members' remuneration, or if I knew nothing about it, I would gather from the hon. member for Assiniboia that he had no expenses at all at home or elsewhere. I would gather that he was making no coverage whatsoever of his riding.
I would assume also from his speech that all ridings in Canada are alike and that the expenses in connection with one are the same as the expenses in connection with all others. Let me say to him that there would be a difference of at least $3,000 a year between providing an adequate coverage for his riding and for my own.
My riding is one of the largest in Canada, occupying as it does a geographical position in the northern part of Saskatchewan. It covers 40 per cent of the physical area of that province. The people are scattered in many remote areas. Some hon. members might say that they did not need to see their member, that they did not need the same service as other people; but that is not my attitude toward my constituents. I feel that the person in the most remote part of my constituency is entitled to see me at least once a year. That is what has always happened as far as I am concerned, and that is what is going to continue to happen-he is going to see me at least once a year.
Ninety per cent of the area of my riding must be covered by plane. As hon. members know, we are away from here for only a few months in the summer and that means that it must be covered by pontoon-equipped
[Mr. Shaw.J

planes. It costs a minimum of $35 an hour for such a plane to fly a short distance, and if you require to fly in the northern areas a plane will cost $70 an hour. I do not want to say to members of this house that you pay for every hour you have a plane. You do it in terms of flying hours and, depending on the type of plane, they have a minimum which they charge per day. To adequately cover my own riding, and it takes from ten to twelve days to cover the remote parts, on the basis of $50 an hour on an average, it costs $3,000 a year to cover the northern area.
I do not believe my constituents are going to suggest they do not want that service, and I do not think they are going to suggest that I pay for it. They do know that in the past I paid a portion of it, and I was able to do so out of the conduct of my own business.
I take the same stand as the hon. member for York South (Mr. Noseworthy), who I think did a very remarkable job in this debate in telling the house and the people of Canada that he is actually worse off by being a member of this house, and that he would be far better off in his profession of teaching where he would get a higher salary. I think the argument that we are getting $10,000 does not hold. Even if we made $25,000 it would not make any more difference, if our expenses ran to $20,000, than if we received a salary of $10,000, and the expenses ran to $5,000. The net result is the same.
It is rather odd to find the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Argue) stating that we have take-home pay of $583 a month. No such pay is obtainable or will be obtainable even if we get $10,000 a year.
I made my position clear in my own riding on many occasions before I ever came down here in 1949, and certainly in this last election campaign. I said then that this very situation might arise, and that definitely I was going to support higher pay for members. In Ottawa here, I am 2,100 miles from home. I found it impossible to continue the business that I carried on until a year ago, and I had to dispose of it. In that position, I am like the hon. member for York South, and the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Shaw), who has just spoken.
I believe this is a full-time job as far as giving full representation to the people we represent is concerned. I have so told my constituents, and I have been elected twice on that very ground, or at least that was part of the reason people voted for me at that time. Certainly I did not hide the light under

a bushel. I made it plain to them I would cover all parts of the riding and would regard the job as a full-time job.
If, as an uninitiated member, I accepted the remarks of the hon. member for Assini-boia I would conclude that as soon as the house rose I would be immediately free to go on holidays. That is not the case. That is when I do my travelling in my own riding, and during that time I cover no less than 20,000 miles. The hon. member for Red Deer mentioned his car and the depreciation on it. I do not believe our constituents expect us to pay these expenses, because we would not travel these distances if we were not members.
The C.C.F. government in the province of Saskatchewan saw fit to raise the pay of provincial members. I have no argument with that. I do not believe they are overpaid. But my own constituency covers the major part of five provincial ridings. They cover that area with provincial members at a cost of $15,000 a year; yet I understand that they sit for only six weeks in the year. Certainly some of them give additional time to covering their own areas, but there is no comparison whatsoever with our position.
If you consider our $10,000 a year on the basis of what the hon. member for Assini-boia said, you earn it during the time here and then you are off on holidays. These provincial members receive $15,000 a year and work for a period of six weeks. We are here seven or eight months, and we will receive $10,000 if the house passes this proposed increase.
I think these remarks set forth my position. Even with the increases now forecast I would definitely be better off in the business I previously had, as far as actual money left over is concerned. I have pointed out that it takes about $3,000 per year for plane travel in my riding. There is at least another $1,000 to cover travel and depreciation on a motor vehicle. The Minister of National Revenue is interested in another couple of thousand dollars, and various other organizations in my riding are interested in small portions which I am pleased to give. If I have a minimum of about $3,500 of actual take-home pay I think I am doing fairly well.
The $10,000 does not mean anything at all. I am interested only in the $3,500, and I would suggest that on the basis of the pay we have been getting here and the services we give to the people of Canada, most of us are making great sacrifices in order to carry out our duties. Certainly I am prepared to go back to the people of the constituency of Meadow Lake and put it to them as to 83276-107*
Senate and House of Commons whether they think $10,000 a year is too much for me, and whether they believe I am telling the truth in outlining my expenses as far as they are concerned. If they do not think so, and if they believe the services I render are not adequate for the money expended, I have no doubt they will dispose of me in the usual and traditional manner.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to deal with one or two points in connection with this bill. As a new member I would not presume to pass any opinion on how much it costs members to stay here and survive, but I think we have heard obviously sincere speeches in this house on this question, even from the members of the group opposite me.
We had one obviously sincere speech from the veteran member for Vancouver-Kingsway (Mr. Maclnnis), who had his own ideas. I thought the most effective speech I heard in the whole debate was that from the hon. member for Cape Breton South (Mr. Gillis), who told a calm unvarnished tale of just what happens to a private member without any backing when he comes into this house.
I will say very frankly that I might have had some reservations about this bill, but they vanished yesterday when it was made very clear that the increased indemnity did not include any increase in members' pensions. Beyond that, I find myself in complete agreement with the principle of this bill. I think that anyone in an executive position on a newspaper, in any business, or in any job in this Dominion of Canada who was asked to rate members' duties and responsibilities in comparison with any similar responsibilities in Canada would say that an indemnity of $8,000 a year was not too much.
While I myself during the course of my life have occasionally taken a crack or two at the place sometimes referred to in this chamber as "the other place", let me say that I for one have no sympathy whatever with the argument I heard within the past few days that since we are going to have the other place we should somehow or other starve them into slow disappearance or strangulation so that perhaps, as in the kids' game, "let the old cat die out".
I believe, on the contrary, the upper chamber is an integral part of this parliament of Canada, and the question is: Do we want our House of Commons to be an efficient and effective organization to serve the people of Canada, and do we want the Senate or upper chamber to be an effective instrument to serve the people of Canada? I would submit just one question, Mr. Speaker, and it is this.
1692	HOUSE OF
Senate and House of Commons Would it contribute to a strong Senate or a weaker Senate if we were to leave the Senate indemnity as it is and raise the House of Commons indemnity 100 per cent?
I think the answer is self-evident. I rise, however, to speak in this debate on one simple point. If I were asked to vote for or against this bill on the ground of whether or not the old age pensioners and those on war veterans allowance were or were not going to get a better deal, then I would certainly stand with those on war veterans allowance and the old age pensioners. As the hon. member for Maeleod (Mr. Hansell) said the other day, if that were the only choice in this house, we would get a 100 per cent vote on that question. If I were asked to name the one thing which I think would be most desirable in this Canada of ours, in order to make it a happier and more prosperous place for all of us, at the head of the list I personally would place more generous allowances for those on war veterans allowance and on old age pensions.
Here in my hand I have clippings from all three Vancouver newspapers of all different stripes of politics. I assure you, Mr. Speaker, that I do not intend to read them at any length. By and large, over a period of months, all three papers of all political stripes have urged the necessity for having the indemnity of members of parliament fixed at a level which will assure the perpetuation of this House of Commons on an efficient basis. I find that all three papers in Vancouver now take much the same line. All of them take the same line. They say that if it is true that our members of parliament require more of indemnity, they should be more receptive to the arguments about the people who are in a much more desperate plight than is anyone in this house, namely the people who are trying to eke out an existence on $40 a month and are living in a state of almost slow or semistarvation. One paper asks:
How can our members of parliament now in the act of practically doubling their own pay justify their neglect of the pensioners in their present plight?
That is the Vancouver News-Herald. The Vancouver Province, which sometimes supports the Conservative party, says:	"M.P.'s
should remember O.A.P.'s", and the editorial ends up in this way:
The M.P.'s generous stipend and the pensioners' pittance come from the same purse. Why is one so handsome? Why is the other so mean?
The paper which writes the most intelligent comment of all, namely the Vancouver Sun, in a very lucid editorial says that there should be a streamlining of all the welfare


payments in Canada, that we should have a dominion-provincial conference to get some kind of order and to tidy up the loose ends of all these things like assistance grants, war veterans allowances, pensions for the blind; and it goes on to show the wide discrepancy there is between the various groups. The editorial is headed "Equalize Payments to Needy, Then Increase Them All".
My point is quite simple, Mr. Speaker. In this vote we are not called on to vote either for a modest and, I think, reasonable increase in the indemnity for members of parliament as against and as a substitute for a more generous outlook towards old age pensions and war veterans allowances. On the contrary, we are asked to decide a very simple question:	Is the member of
parliament worthy of an indemnity which enables him to stay here and to survive? When the majority of this house votes a decisive yes, I submit that by that decisive yes vote they are establishing a principle that if the member of parliament is worthy of a survival indemnity, then that same principle applies to all other elements in Canada, this great country of ours; and instead of its being a less generous outlook toward old age pensioners and those on war veterans allowance, I submit it is an indication of better things to come as soon as this country can afford it.

Most members from British Columbia have spoken, and the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway (Mr. Maclnnis), in his usual honest manner, has made his stand. Because I am a Liberal member from British Columbia who represents more C.C.F. supporters than does anyone else on this side of the house, I think I too should take my stand because there will be some discussion at home with regard to this matter.
I think the honest point of view with regard to a member of parliament is that he should say what he has to say here and nowhere else. I am going to support this bill, and I am going to do so on one premise perhaps more than on any other. In his speech yesterday the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) brought to the attention of this house the dignity of a member of parliament; and in doing that he did not refer to the dignity of a member of parliament only during a session of parliament but rather to the dignity of a member of parliament for twelve months of the year. My riding demands a twelve-month service. Not only am I serving here but when I go home I have an office in my home to which anyone can come at any

time and tell me his problems. As I understand it, the method of payment under this bill will be one by which we shall secure the money every thirty days. I think that is only right and proper.
One other thing I wish to mention is the fact that some members of the C.C.F. party- as represented by the speech of the leader of the party who, I am glad to see, is in the house at the moment-tell me that they are going to support a $2,000 increase. I wonder how much the viewpoint of the leader of the C.C.F. is reflected in that $2,000 increase. I believe that this matter has been considered by their caucus or by some meeting and that this is a compromise between consciences. I point out to you, Mr. Speaker, that there has been no denial from the party when I said that. I quite understand the position.

speechtext:
Before the question is put, Mr. Speaker, I should like to say one word. Once again I think there has been a considerable amount of confusion with regard to this matter. When the division is called and we are voting, what are we voting on? We are voting on the principle of the bill. We are not voting on the details of that bill. There may be disagreement among us with regard to the details, but are we or are we not in favour of a principle, namely, shall the indemnities of members of parliament be increased?
I have no hesitation in saying that I am going to vote for the principle of this bill.
Senate and House of Commons I have felt-and I have said so for a good many years-that members of parliament whom I have known in this house have made personal sacrifices that should not be expected of members of parliament who represent any constituencies in Canada.
A great deal has been said about what is being said in the country, and so on and so forth. I am going to say this. Yesterday, by fortuitous circumstance, I saw in the gallery an outstanding farmer who lives just across the border of my constituency. I saw him listening intently to the debate all afternoon. I went up into the gallery about half past five and asked him what he thought about this. He said, "Well, it is about time members of parliament had something of this sort done for them." Last evening I met two other outstanding farmers from my province, one of them from my own constituency. They occupy important positions in the agricultural organizations of which they are members. I asked them the same question, and I got precisely the same answer.
I know that, so far as the executive in my own constituency are concerned, they know exactly what membership in this house involves. They know that the proposal to increase indemnities is warranted by the circumstances under which we have operated in this house. I have no hesitation in voting for the principle of this bill. As I said in my address the other day, I am not in agreement with some of the details of this bill and I shall say so when the time comes. This is not the time. If any hon. member in this house believes that the indemnity should be increased, that hon. member should rise in his place and support the bill. My hon. friends of the official opposition say they are going to oppose this bill.
Last Friday evening we had before us a motion for second reading of a bill in connection with the housing act. There was bitter opposition to the details of that bill from this side of the house. When the vote was called all of us on this side of the house, with two exceptions, voted for that bill. We did not vote for the details of the bill. I did not like some of the details. I rose in my place and voted for that bill because I believed in the principle of the bill.
I say to my hon. friends that exactly the same situation faces the house at this moment. If we are going to vote we shall vote for the principle and not the details, just as last Friday evening when members who had bitterly criticized the housing bill rose in their places and supported the principle of that bill. Members of this house who believe, as I think most hon. members do believe,
1694	HOUSE OF
Senate and House of Commons that there should be an increase in this indemnity should get up and show where they stand by voting for the bill.

speechtext:
should like briefly to put my personal position on the record, Mr. Speaker, with regard to this matter. First of all I may say, sir, that I support the general objective of this bill, that objective being to so improve the financial aspect of service in this parliament that the government of Canada may be served better by attracting men of talent across this nation to serve in parliament. However, I am voting against this bill because I disagree with the method, and I do not like the contents of the act as it will stand if this bill is passed in its present form.
Before listing three of the objections I have, may I say that as a comparative newcomer to this house with service of something over a year at the time of the last general election, I had to make a decision as to whether or not I could afford to continue in parliament should it be the desire of the people of Calgary South to re-elect me. After a fairly careful study of the situation I found that during my first term in parliament I was a subsidized member. I was subsidized by myself and by my business to the extent that for every single dollar I drew as a member of parliament I had to take from my personal assets or my business more than $3.
In the light of those circumstances I feel quite firm in my conviction that the present indemnity is far from adequate. I do not think any of us in this house should be required to draw heavily upon our personal resources, nor should we be forced into the position of having our business subsidize us in our service to the public of Canada.
However, sir, I come now to the three points which I feel would be wrong in the Senate and House of Commons Act should this particular bill pass in its present form. My first objection is to the tax-free expense allowance. I believe, sir, that all payments received by members of parliament should be taxable income. I believe that our earnings as members should be treated in exactly the same way as the earnings of other citizens in this country. I believe there should be provision for a deduction from income tax for a member's legitimate expenses in carrying out his duties.
Then, sir, I do not like the loose rules covering attendance. I believe that in any general revision of the Senate and House of Commons Act steps should be taken to tighten up the rules which are now honoured in some degree more in the breach than in
[Mr. Coldwell.)

the observance. I might say that I have been absent on a number of occasions during my two years in Ottawa. I have not yet drawn a full sessional indemnity. In my own rather strict interpretation of these rules I have believed that my time devoted to travel back home on matters not entirely related to my work as a member is time for which I should not charge the public of Canada. This is one phase of the subsidy which my business pays toward keeping me here.
Finally, sir, I do not believe that, despite the many fine men who have served and are still serving in the Senate, the duties and functions of the Senate justify treating the members on the same financial basis as the members of the House of Commons.
With these objections in mind, sir, I trust the government will reconsider its decision and withdraw this bill for further, independent study to determine what complete and detailed amendments to the Senate and House of Commons Act might best be submitted to this parliament in order to achieve, on a sounder basis, the general objectives involved in Bill No. 171.

We are considering a motion for the second reading of this bill, when it is the principle of the bill that is submitted for approval or disapproval, and when it does not mean that those who vote for the bill are voting for everything the bill contains. As the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar clearly indicated, that was illustrated in the conduct of hon. members in this house no longer ago than last week when after, I think, four days of critical debate of the contents of the housing bill, one amending the housing act and making further provision to encourage housing, that bill was approved by the vote of all but two members of the house. It was a vote in which not all those who had spoken took part; but very many of those who had been critical of the bill did vote in favour of second reading.
That is the situation here. A vote for the second reading of the bill will be a vote to confirm a principle that many have declared their intention of voting against, although one they agree with, namely that there should be some increase, some revision upward of the indemnity of members of this house. One

would gather from the tone in which they expressed their intention to vote negatively on second reading that, notwithstanding, they do expect that second reading will be passed, and that their vote will not mean the end of the bill.
There is one other point that I do wish to mention again. Our constitutional system being what it is, the government felt it should not come to parliament recommending a bill that would provide for a more substantial indemnity for members of this house than for members of the other house. It is quite true that in all the reasons we have giveh in attempting to justify an increase in the indemnities or allowances of members of this house, we have given reasons that apply to members of this house and do not apply to the same extent-I am free to confess it- to members of the other house.
This bill, if and when it is passed by this house, will go to the other house; and if the members of the other house were themselves to say that, taking into consideration the reasons that motivated the increase here, and the fact that many of them do not apply to their situation, they would not feel it proper to have the same indemnity provided for them, I am sure if it came back in that shape to this house, this house would agree.
But I am not asking this house, nor am I suggesting that this house should take the position, that it will not agree to a similar indemnity being provided for all members of parliament. And members of the other house are members of parliament, just as we are. I am not suggesting that this house would not agree to their being treated in the same way.
Now, that is the situation. I repeat that I am not asking any member of this house, on whichever side he may sit, to vote yes on this motion because I make the motion and because the government recommends this bill. Again I think it is the responsibility of each one of us to express his own honest conviction as to whether or not there should be an increase.
