speakeroldname: Mr. A. M. Campbell (The Balllefords) moved
subsubtopic: PROPOSED AMENDMENT TO ENLARGE SCOPE
speechtext:
the second reading of Bill No. 175, to amend the Navigable Waters Protection Act (protection of rivers).
He said: Mr. Speaker, never have I stood in the House of Commons to discuss a matter which has affected me more or given me more concern than the matter I propose to discuss at the present time.
I expect most people know the value of water to health, but perhaps some people do not know what it is to do without a good drink of water. Perhaps some people do not know what it means to have to go without water and to be really thirsty. I know from experience that one of the greatest discomforts anyone can have is to be without a proper supply of water. I once travelled over the western plains and went without a good drink of water for as long as two weeks, and when we came across a spring the whole caravan I was travelling with stopped, lay down and put their heads in that stream, took their fill and then went back time and again to enjoy that pure water.
In my constituency today thousands of people have no decent water to drink. The people mostly affected are in the town of Battleford and in the mental hospital in the city of North Battleford. Something has happened to the water supply in the North Saskatchewan river at the present time, and no one seems to know what it is.
83276-108J
Navigable Waters Protection Act
The hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker) has brought this matter up on a number of occasions and had asked the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Martin) several questions along these lines. Up to date we have no knowledge of what has happened to the water of the North Saskatchewan river, but we do know that it is in such a state that the people living along that river in the city of North Battleford, in the town of Battleford, in Prince Albert, and again in The Pas are unable to get a decent drink of water unless they bring it in from outside.
I say, Mr. Speaker, that this is a horrible situation. I say it is time this parliament did something about it. I want to put on record some of the things that are happening in the town of Battleford. I have here a long letter I received from a housewife telling me of the conditions in that town. She writes:
After all the conferences and correspondence and travelling back and forth the latest thing to be announced is that Premier Douglas has written a personal letter to Premier Manning telling him Alberta is responsible for the pollution.
Some industries in the province of Alberta have been dumping some sort of element into this water which is poisoning the water or making it unfit for human use. This lady's letter continues:
Meanwhile the water situation here is worse if anything. In the past two weeks several children had to be taken home from school when they became ill after drinking the water while many older persons have had gastro-intestinal trouble and have been advised by the doctor not to drink the water. Most people are boiling the water but that doesn't solve the problem in the schools where children are bound to get thirsty and what are they to do?
Now, Mr. Speaker, if we are to have healthy children they must have an adequate supply of good, pure water. Those hon. members who have raised families can all remember how many times their children would go over to the tap or to the water pail to quench their thirst. Here we have the situation that the children in these towns are unable to get a good drink of water.
The letter goes on:
The people in town and at the Saskatchewan hospital-those who live on the grounds that is-are getting their water in containers either from friends in the country, North Battleford or the irrigation hospital where the water supply is taken from the Battle river. The mayor and the local doctor, J. E. Nunn, both told me they can't and won't drink the water.
I want to draw attention to the fact that patients in the mental hospital are unable to obtain a supply of fresh water. The attendants and members of the staff are able to get in their cars and drive out into the country where they can obtain good water,

Navigable Waters Protection Act but the patients, these people who are ill, these people who cannot understand why the water does not taste good, are being subjected to bad psychological effects which will certainly retard their recovery from their present ailments.
This letter I have already quoted from goes on to relate how a couple of high school boys have been operating a small laboratory for some time past. They took some of this water and distilled it and after distillation all that was left was a yellowish residue. The letter continues:
The water supply at North Battleford has not been affected yet but in checking with F. Holliday, the water engineer, I was told they felt it was only a matter of time until North Battleford would have the same trouble. You see their wells are situated far enough back from the river that when the water level drops down and when it freezes over, no water flows through the back channel to get into the wells.
I might say in this connection, Mr. Speaker, that the water level of the Saskatchewan river is extremely low at the present time. I do not know how long this rubbish, or whatever it is, has been dumped into the river at the city of Edmonton, but obviously it has been going on for a year or more, and it is quite possible that with the water at a high level whatever was put into the river was diluted sufficiently so that it did not cause the trouble which has now developed.
I quote again from this letter:
The one place which has had the most trouble and of which barely anything has been said, is the provincial hospital across the river.
That is the mental hospital. The writer of the letter goes on to say something of what the patients in that mental hospital have to put up with. They cannot get a drink of water without being nauseated and made ill in many cases. The letter goes on:
I have checked with Dr. Nunn and he said the incidence of gastro-intestinal trouble in Battleford has definitely risen in the past month. My own ten year old son was brought home last week from school. He has been drinking only boiled water and was warned against drinking water at school. He became so thirsty one morning, however, that he simply had to have a drink and little more than an hour later, he was brought home, sick to his stomach and with severe abdominal cramps. That's the way it affects you, apparently. Many people thought they had stomach flu' and it also causes dysentry, I am told. I heard of a case yesterday where a small child of a provincial hospital employee is in hospital. Apparently she has an allergy to whatever the element in the water is and every time she drinks it she breaks out in a terrible rash and her face swells up. All these things seem to be rather trivial but I feel very strongly that the human element is the one thing that must not be overlooked in this controversy.
Now, Mr. Speaker, when the matter was put to the Minister of National Health and


Welfare several times during the session he stated the federal government was not competent to do anything about the matter.
I shall now deal with my proposed amendment to the bill. As the bill states, this is an act to amend the Navigable Waters Protection Act which is for the protection of rivers. Section 18 of the act, as it is at present, reads as follows:
No owner or tenant of any saw-mill, or any workman therein or other person shall throw or cause to be thrown, or suffer or permit to be thrown any sawdust, edgings, slabs, bark or rubbish of any description whatsoever into any river, stream or other water, any part of which is navigable or which flows into any navigable water.
There is no doubt that this act was passed many years ago, before industrial plants were built on rivers. I want to direct attention to the fact that the city of Edmonton in particular, in common with many other parts of Canada, is becoming highly industrialized. I can remember driving not many miles north of the city of Ottawa when I passed a plant, and I was hardly past it until I noticed a stream of whitish-looking liquid running away from the plant, under the highway and into the Gatineau river.
This matter of dumping this sort of stuff into rivers is becoming of great concern to many of our people. When the government built the Chalk River plant I notice that they took care to see to it that a ditch was dug and that the residue from that plant was taken away from the river into a swamp not far from the plant.
The situation has changed. The present navigable waters act is a federal act which gives this government jurisdiction over any navigable waters in Canada, and prohibits a saw mill from throwing rubbish of any description whatsoever into any river, stream or other water, any part of which is navigable or which flows into any navigable water. I have looked up the definition of "rubbish" in the large Oxford dictionary. "Rubbish" is defined as waste or refuse material, debris, litter, refuse; rejected and useless matter of any kind.
The first point I wish to make tonight is that this government is competent to prevent the dumping by saw mills of rubbish into navigable streams. The act discriminates against saw mills. A saw mill is the only industry which, under the act, is prohibited from dumping rubbish into a river. Any other industry can build on river banks and dump all its rubbish or all its refuse into a navigable river without any hindrance from this government. My amendment to this act would expand the scope of the act to the

extent of adding the words "or other industrial plant". Section 18 would then read:
No owner or tenant of any saw-mill, or other industrial plant, or any workman therein or other person shall throw or cause to be thrown, or suffer or permit to be thrown any sawdust, edgings, slabs, bark or rubbish of any description whatsoever into any river, stream or other water, any part of which is navigable or which flows into any navigable water.
On January 19 the hon. member for Prince Albert asked the Minister of National Health and Welfare what action the federal government intends to take to preserve from pollution the waters of rivers that flow through two or more provinces. In his reply, as reported at page 1235 of Hansard, the minister stated:
The responsibility for remedying the situation is recognized by both provinces as not coming within the competence of the federal government.
He went on further to say:
Indeed, whether or not there was that acknowledgment I would have to submit that would have to be the situation as far as the federal government is concerned, for this is clearly a matter that does not come within the competence of the federal government.
I cannot understand the attitude taken by the minister. Here we have a terrible situation where thousands of people are concerned. Water is of primary importance to the health of our people, and we have a situation where one or more industries are dumping their refuse and rubbish into the Saskatchewan river at Edmonton in the province of Alberta. Pollution of the Saskatchewan river in the province of Alberta does not affect the people of Alberta directly, because no water is used out of the river below Edmonton until it gets to Battleford and North Battleford in Saskatchewan. The citizens of the town of Battleford use the river as their sole water supply. The mental institution in North Battleford, housing some 2,000 patients besides the staff, depends on this water for human consumption. The river then continues on till it comes to Prince Albert, a city of some 6,000 or 7,000 people. Again these people have to put up with a terrible situation.

speechtext:
I stand corrected. I understand from the hon. member for Prince Albert that the population of the city of Prince Albert is 20,000. That emphasizes my case, Mr. Speaker. From there the river runs on into Manitoba, through The Pas and into Hudson bay.
I would point out that this matter which is put into rivers does not respect provincial boundaries. This river runs through three provinces, and the minister says the federal
Navigable Waters Protection Act government has no jurisdiction or is not competent to deal with the matter. Surely it is time this parliament took action to stop the dumping of whatever element it is that is being dumped into the river at Edmonton. I should like to ask the Minister of National Health and Welfare why it should not come within the competence of the federal government, if the federal government expects that a conference is going to have to be held after damage has been done to a river which may take years to clear up. It may take years to clear the situation up because of the fact that the water is very low and this matter, whatever it is, is no doubt soaking and working itself down into the silt; it may take only months or it might take years before this river is able to clear itself. We should have legislation in our federal statutes so these rivers can be policed to make sure that no industry will be allowed, under federal law, to dump its refuse into navigable waters or streams that are being used or might some day be used for human consumption.
In the question asked by the hon. member for Prince Albert on January 19 he stated that he had brought this matter to the attention of the department some three weeks previously, so the department would know of the situation on or about December 20. On January 25 the hon. member for Prince Albert, as reported at page 1407 of Hansard, asked the following question:
I should like to direct a question to the Minister of National Health and Welfare, bringing to his attention again the emergent situation, in Prince Albert and also in North Battleford, which is becoming more serious rather than better. In an editorial I have here in my hand I see a description of conditions of the water at Prince Albert. Those who speak with authority describe it as "water comparable to low grade swamp wash laced with crude oil."
In view of the fact that this situation has continued for a considerable period of time, I would ask the minister what stand the federal government is taking with reference to this matter and the removal of this nuisance, or at least to give assistance in that direction. I would also ask whether, under all the circumstances, regardless of federal responsibility or otherwise, he would make available and send out to Prince Albert one or two of his officials to see what they can do to solve the problem there and to preserve the health of the people. The situation is serious.
The Minister of National Health and Welfare replied as follows:
My hon. friend does not now deal with the question of competence. That was dealt with in the question which he put to me the other day. He now asks me if we would be prepared to send out to the provinces of Alberta and Saskatchewan officials of our own department who are technically qualified to assist in this matter. I am happy to be able to inform my hon. friend that not only will we be able to do so but that we have already done so. Last Friday the supervising engineer of the public

Navigable Waters Protection Act health engineering division of our department attended a meeting in Edmonton with the representative of the company and the department of health, and the matter was fully reviewed. The technical officers, including our own officials, are now engaged in determining the precise cause of the pollution. The supervising engineer has also been in touch with the officials of the department of health in Regina. My hon. friend may be assured that, without in any way begging the question of competence, the federal government will do all it can do to assist the provincial authorities to carry out their constitutional responsibility.
The hon. member for Prince Albert replied to the minister as follows:
I thank the minister for his reply, and I should like to ask a supplementary question. The other day I asked him to ascertain the responsibility of the federal government in connection with rivers that traverse two or more provinces. Has he had any legal opinion on that matter? Is it not a fact that, under the situation disclosed here, there is a distinct responsibility federally to look into this matter and to act?
The minister replied:
I do not believe I can add anything to what I said in answer to the supplementary question put to me by my hon. friend about four or five days ago.
The Minister of National Health and Welfare, in reply to the question of the hon. member for Prince Albert on January 19, stated, as reported at page 1235 of Hansard for that date:
My hon. friend will find that this matter-I do not mean this particular situation but the principles involved-was fully discussed in the house in 1949, and the discussion can be found at page 571 of Hansard of October 6 of that year.
The discussion to which the minister referred related to an amendment moved by the hon. member for York West (Mr. Adamson) to section 19 of the Navigable Waters Protection Act, and had to do with the pollution of the waters along the shore line of lake Ontario, while the case which I am arguing refers to a river running through three provinces. During that debate the Minister of Transport (Mr. Chevrier) argued that the federal government was not competent to deal with the situation, and the amendment was voted down. I believe the minister was correct, because this is a completely different situation.
Again on January 28 the minister referred to the matter of competence in reply to a question of mine as to whether or not he had received a report from the supervising engineer of the public health engineering division concerning the pollution of the North Saskatchewan river. At the time the minister said he had nothing to add to the reply he had made to the hon. member for Prince Albert a few days previously.
In a press report received from Prince Albert a few days ago it was stated that this


condition has been continuing since November 15 last. Surely it is time this federal government accepted the responsibility of looking after the health of our people, and corrected this situation which has been known since last November.
Another press report states that health minister Cross of Alberta stated last Tuesday that a dam on the North Saskatchewan river 100 miles west of Edmonton had been mentioned as a possible solution to the pollution of the river waters. It was estimated this dam would cost between $3 and $4 million. I should like to ask this house who would pay for a dam of that description? Would the people of Canada be asked to put up between $3 and $4 million in order to avoid the pollution of the river by some industries? I am sure that this condition is not limited to Saskatchewan, but that industries are doing the same thing in other parts of the country.
Health minister Cross goes on to suggest that such a dam would permit control of the river level in winter periods of low water when there is greater risk of pollution. If we had a federal law that would prevent the cause of pollution there would be no necessity for building dams or forcing our people to drink such horrible water. Another press report from Prince Albert reads as follows:
Local water drinkers can expect to have tasteless water again in approximately one week, it was reported at Monday night's meeting of city council. The North Saskatchewan river, from which this city draws its drinking water, has been polluted by industrial wastes from Alberta since early last November.
A report by J. G. Schaeffer, chief sanitation officer to the provincial health department, revealed that the addition of chlorine dioxide to the water would remove the taste and smell. The chemical treatment was discovered after extensive tests were made on samples of river water taken right at the site of the Edmonton factory blamed for the nuisance.
Here we are going to have another horrible element added to the water in an effort to counteract the elements that are causing the pollution. This sort of thing has been going on in the United States for many years. They have arrived at the point where most of their rivers are polluted to such an extent that the water is not fit for human consumption. The estimated cost of the treatment of industrial wastes from major industries contributing to the pollution of surface water in the United States is $694 million. The source of my information is a pamphlet entitled "Water Pollution in the United States", pages 31, 53 and 54.
Because of the rapid expansion of industry in Canada, especially in the province of

Alberta, this problem will become more and more aggravated unless this parliament agrees to take action to stop the pollution of our rivers at the source. The problem will not be solved permanently by building dams or by adding more and more chemicals to the polluted waters.
I hope the government will agree that the time has come to take definite action. If they are not prepared to support this bill, and if they have a better method of tackling the problem, I hope they will reveal it to the house now. Surely it is the duty of this parliament to make sure our people are not subjected to possible sickness or disease merely because parliament has refused to face up to the problem.
I have informed the house what the problem is, Mr. Speaker, and I have made suggestions. I hope the Minister of Transport or some other minister will either agree to accept this bill or come forward with a better proposition.

subsubtopic: PROPOSED AMENDMENT TO ENLARGE SCOPE
speechtext:
First I wish to congratulate the hon. member for The Battlefords (Mr. Campbell) upon having introduced this amendment. Few members in this house have any realization of the situation which prevails in the cities of North Battleford and Prince Albert, and in the town of The Pas.
The people in the city of Prince Albert were the first to have this problem. As a result of the dumping of deleterious substances into the river below Edmonton, 50,000 people in Saskatchewan are indirectly affected and 30,000 people are in the position that they cannot drink the water which flows in the Saskatchewan river. "Water, water, everywhere, nor any drop to drink"; that is the position of these people. As the hon. member has pointed out, this has become a national emergency. If not met as a national emergency, it will become a permanent problem for the people along the northern Saskatchewan. There is no description of the bad odour of the water that is more fitting than the words of Shakespeare when he said:
The rankest compound of villainous smell that ever offended nostril.
That is what we are putting up with on the northern Saskatchewan. Everyone seems to contend that someone else must accept the constitutional responsibility. We in Prince Albert were the first to suffer. My hon. friend's city of North Battleford and town of Battleford did not come into the picture for several weeks because of the location of the water intake in these two urban municipalities. Prince Albert has experienced
Navigable Waters Protection Act this situation since November 12. An appeal was made to the provincial government of Saskatchewan and the stand was in effect that it was not a provincial problem.
The inception of it is in Alberta. The department of health in Alberta has taken a benevolent interest in the subject, and says in effect "This is not our problem". Recently the province of Manitoba has made representations because the problem has finally reached The Pas. Certainly this is a national problem, and something must be done to meet it.
I am not going to quote newspaper references extensively, but while my hon. friend was speaking I sent to the library to secure the Prince Albert Daily Herald so I could give the house something of the picture, and in a few minutes show the conditions prevailing there. I find that in the issue of January 29 this newspaper states:
Manitoba and Alberta have asked federal aid in ridding North Saskatchewan river of pollution. Request from Manitoba came to federal government when The Pas appealed to Manitoba government for aid in clearing up a water condition similar to one prevalent in Prince Albert.
In letter to city council from Hon. Paul Martin, federal minister of health, it was stated that results of tests on water from the river are not yet available.
The federal health minister has twice stated in the House of Commons that solution of water problem is not responsibility of federal government.
Prince Albert is asking for some action. On the 28th of January officials from the federal and provincial authorities met there. The heading of the article on that date is "Officials Here to Talk Water." They talked water, and while they talked the people thirsted. And that has been the condition that has continued for a period of almost two and a half months.
I could go back day by day in this newspaper file, and find each day a reference to the situation. Someone says, "Why do not these cities do something to meet the situation themselves?" The city of Prince Albert has made some investigation into the question and has found that it would be financially impracticable for the city to handle this problem alone, as was pointed out by the superintendent of utilities. He said it would cost the city at least $60 a day to meet a problem that results from a condition of affairs outside of and beyond the city, and also beyond the province of Saskatchewan.
Day by day the city council of Prince Albert has been asking for action, and the health authorities and representatives of the various western provinces have been discussing the matter. The people of Prince Albert

Navigable Waters Protection Act depend for their water supply upon what can be obtained from wells in the neighbourhood. I wonder at the self-restraint that has been shown in trying to get action.
The answer by the federal authorities has been in effect: Are we, in effect, our brother's keeper, under the legislative distribution of powers in this dominion? Certainly it is not the government of Saskatchewan that is alone responsible, nor is it the government of Alberta, and the government of Manitoba has no direct responsibility.
I make an appeal to the minister to brush aside for the moment some of these constitutional difficulties that can be raised on every occasion and on every matter in respect of the distributed powers of legislative authority. Give us assistance. I repeat that the hon. member for The Battlefords deserves high commendation for offering this amendment. I am wondering, though, whether it would actually cover the situation. The section as amended would read:
No owner or tenant of any saw-mill, or other industrial plant, or any workman therein or other person shall throw or cause to be thrown, or suffer or permit to be thrown any sawdust, edgings, slabs, bark or rubbish of any description whatsoever into any river, stream or other water, any part of which is navigable or which flows into any navigable water.
This section would create a new offence. As it is today I do not think there is any offence under the law covering the problem I have described; for certainly what is being dumped into the river is not sawdust, edgings, slabs, bark or rubbish of any description. And those latter words would be interpreted, I would say, in their relationship to the words preceding them.
If this amendment were carried, I think there would still be no offence created to cover the prevalent situation. Having that in mind, and subject to my hon. friend's agreement, I suggest that these further words be added to section 18 in question, the additional words to begin after the word "whatsoever" in the fifth line of section 18. Those words would be, "or chemicals of any kind, and without restricting the generality of the foregoing any substance which, although not deleterious or harmful to human health, causes discomfort or annoyance to users of water".
This would make it an offence which would cover the situation in question, the one we face. I am not going to talk this bill out, although I could say a great deal more. This problem has continued since November 12. Anything I have done in bringing it to the attention of the house has not been done in any critical attitude. I

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, while we are still on clause 2 there is another aspect of the matter which I wish to ask the house to consider. As hon. members are aware, the clause now before us provides for the proposed increase to be made available to senators and to members of the House of Commons. I am aware of the position the Prime Minister has taken with respect to this matter, namely that he feels the Senate is here to stay as part of our constitutional set-up and that so long as this is the case they should be treated on a basis of equality with the members of the House of Commons.
I do not agree with that position. As a matter of fact, I might point out that even in terms of dollars and cents the respective positions have not been equal since 1945. When Mr. King first brought in a resolution regarding expense allowances, if my memory serves me correctly, these allowances were to be provided only for the members of the House of Commons. Later, after newspaper reports to the effect the Senate would not agree to the proposition if it were passed in that form, Mr. King withdrew the resolution and placed another one on the order paper. It provided for the expense allowance to be paid to members of both houses but made a distinction or a difference, namely that in the case of members of the House of Commons, except cabinet ministers and the Leader of the Opposition, that $2,000 would be tax free but in the case of senators it was to be taxable. Hence in terms of actual dollars and cents there is a difference already, and I suggest that fact invalidates the argument that we have to be kept on a basis of equality.
It has also been pointed out that, in so far
as the Prime Minister contends that the

parliament at Westminster is a model for us to pay some attention to, the members of the House of Lords serve without any indemnity paid directly from the exchequer of that country. Most of us feel that there is a tremendous difference between the amount of work that has to be done by members of the House of Commons and the amount of work that has to be done by members of the other place. I think it is significant that in the editorial columns of the newspapers of this country during the past week or so considerable opposition has been expressed -indeed, from quite unexpected sources- against this increase being given to Their Honours in the other place.
I am sure the Prime Minister was not surprised this afternoon when the house smiled somewhat at his suggestion that we send the bill over to them with the increase for members of both houses written into it, and leave it to them to reduce it if they saw fit. The number of amendments which Their Honours make to important bills is not great; and the likelihood of their proposing such an amendment is, I suggest, somewhat remote. But whether or not that is the case, it seems to me that we in this chamber have a responsibility to decide whether, as a matter of public policy, an increase to a total of $10,000 should be made with regard to the members of the other house at the same time it is being made with respect to members of the House of Commons. Although it may be the Prime Minister's view that this should be done, it seems to me that the House of Commons should have an opportunity to decide whether or not, in our judgment, that is good public policy.
In order to give this committee an opportunity to decide whether or not this increase should be made with respect to members of both houses, I propose to move an amendment to clause 2 of the bill. I direct your attention, Mr. Chairman, to the wording of this amendment because, of necessity, one has to draft it in such a manner as to fit into the clause which is before us. My amendment is:
That section 2 of Bill No. 171 be amended by deleting from line 19 the word "and" and by substituting therefor the words "a sessional allowance at the rate of four thousand dollars per annum and to every member of the".
That is the end of the amendment, but it would be only fair for me to read the subsection as it would appear as amended, so that it will make sense not only to persons who may read Hansard but to members who are listening to me at the present time. The subsection as amended would then read as follows:
For the sessions of each parliament there shall be paid to every member of the Senate a sessional
Senate and House of Commons allowance at the rate of four thousand dollars per annum and to every member of the House of Commons a sessional allowance at the rate of eight thousand dollars per annum.
I wish to make it clear, Mr. Chairman, that with respect to the latter figure-I refer to the figure of $8,000 per annum for members of the House of Commons-that is not the figure that I think should be there, but that figure has now been decided by two votes of the members of the House of Commons. So far as the former figure is concerned-and I refer to the figure of $4,000 per annum as a sessional allowance for members of the Senate-again I am not picking that figure out of a hat. That is their allowance at the present time. Therefore the effect of my amendment is to provide that Their Honours in the other place be not given the increase which this bill provides for members of the House of Commons.

speechtext:
The Leader of the Opposition said that something should be done by way of investigation, but that suggestion was not accepted. Certainly the reasons why our indemnity should be increased have no application in their entirety to similar increases for members of the Senate. I am going to quote from the Leader-Post, a Liberal paper published in Regina. The editorial is entitled "Enough is Enough". After dealing with the tremendous increases asked for in our indemnities, the editorial goes on to say:
Even more open to question is the proposal for senators also receiving an increase in their indemnities which, with the $2,000 taxable allowance, will bring their annual pay to $10,000. They do not have to go to the expense of fighting elections. Their less onerous duties keep them sitting only a portion of the time that the House of Commons requires. Generally speaking, a senatorial appointment is a help and not a handicap to senators in carrying on their private affairs.
The arguments that have been advanced with such power and eloquence in support of our increases certainly do not apply to the adoption of a similar rate for the other place. As the Leader of the Opposition has said, much is said of the British system, but members of the House of Lords receive no

indemnities. It is for that reason the Regina Leader-Post ended this editorial by saying:
There is, however, merit in the proposal that it be placed before a parliamentary committee for thorough consideration instead of being railroaded through parliament.
This is the comment of a Liberal newspaper which, while disagreeing with the question of a royal commission, supports in general the stand taken by my leader. Give public opinion a chance. A few days ago the pension privileges would not have been dealt with had strong opposition not been taken by us on this side of the house. Public opinion was aroused. A few nights ago the Prime Minister would give almost no consideration to the question. Then public opinion was aroused, and public opinion still rules in this country.
I say to you, sir, that even now the setting up of a committee such as is suggested in that editorial would give an opportunity for the Canadian people to speak. This time parliamentary action is so far ahead of public opinion that it has never been equalled during the period I have been here. In other words in a matter such as this we hasten, but when other questions come before the house the answer is so often that we must wait for public opinion.
Certainly the arguments that were made as to the detrimental effect upon the high standard of the House of Commons if there is no increase in indemnity have no application to the other place. I suggest once more a reconsideration of the proposition advanced by the Leader of the Opposition, which at least would give public opinion an opportunity to be heard. The public would have an opportunity of voicing its disapproval, as the public's disapproval was voiced when it was generally understood that the pension act was not to be amended.

speechtext:
Yesterday when the leader of this group was speaking to this measure he stated that when the proper time came he would propose an amendment, and indicated what kind of amendment this would be. It appears that the time has now arrived, and that the amendment can be moved on this section of the bill. We are sorry the leader of this group is unable to be here this evening, having another rather important speaking engagement.
I confess that I was somewhat disturbed and I am still somewhat disturbed, as I think all must be, when members oppose a measure of this kind, which they may think is unpopular, yet at the same time accept the advantages of the legislation. This leads
Senate and House of Commons me to say that I do not know whether it is popular or unpopular. I can only go by the correspondence I have personally received; and I stated when I spoke on the resolution that my correspondence would indicate that there was not too great opposition to it.
If there is any unpopularity in the country in reference to the measure, those who favour it would take the chance of being unpopular; yet those who may oppose it, thinking they will become popular, are in a position where they can take advantage of it at the expense of those who are in favour of it. That disturbs me.
The hon. member for Yorkton in his speech a few moments ago stated that the cost of living had risen in this country and that there were many people, particularly those on pensions and receiving other social service benefits, who found it extremely hard to get through. I know that. We all know that. And as I said before, if it were a choice between our receiving this increase and that part of the population receiving an additional amount, then I think we would all oppose it, and we would let them have it.
But that is not the case. It is not going to make any difference to them whatsoever. The hon. member for Yorkton on that basis said that it was morally wrong to adopt it. Let me say to him that in my opinion it is morally wrong to oppose it, and then accept it. One hon. member this afternoon, referring to the measure brought down some years ago granting a tax-free allowance, said that when asked if he would accept it he said he would, for the simple reason that it became law, and that he had a perfect right to what was law. I am not going to argue that point at all; I think perhaps he is right there. And I would not say anyone would hide behind the law; I do not think they would.
But I believe there is a way of expressing this in law so that members can refuse to take the additional amount, and yet be within the law. If this measure goes through, as in all probability it will, those who oppose it can use the same argument: "Well, it became law, and I am entitled to it". Yes, that is so. But it is a law which those who oppose it will be able to take advantage of. We think those who oppose the measure should be in a position to show by their actions that they conscientiously oppose it, by being within the law in their active opposition.
Therefore, Mr. Chairman, I move the following amendment:
That clause 2, section 33 (1), be amended by adding at the end thereof the following:
Except that for the sessions of the twenty-second parliament there shall be paid to every member

Senate and House of Commons of the Senate and House of Commons a sessional allowance at the rate of four thousand dollars per annum, plus such portion of an additional four thousand dollars per annum as he may elect to apply for in writing to the treasury officer not later than thirty days after this act comes into force.

I submit the time will come when we will know who are the wrong-way Corrigans. I think they are all on the other side of the house.
In the first place, for those who oppose the increase in the indemnity this motion of course means nothing at all, because if we are voting against an increase, then we have already expressed our opinion as to what the law should be. Therefore this does not enter into the situation at all. For those who are in favour of the increase, however, there might be something in it, because I am sure they are going to think about it and they will change their minds before very long.
However, to speak more seriously on the matter, let me point out, sir, that if there is any logic at all behind this motion, then certainly the same argument and the same logic could be applied to every vote that we take in this house. The hon. member for Macleod prefaced his argument by saying that this measure may be unpopular. He did not know whether it was or not, but he felt that some hon. members may be opposing it because it is unpopular. That same argument could be made on every motion that is put forward in this house, and that is just the grand over-all way of imputing motives to every hon. member who votes on this motion.
In the first place, I do not believe it is the duty of any hon. member, or that it is even the privilege of any hon. member, to doubt the sincerity of any other hon. member in this house; and certainly this motion in the way it is phrased, and the speech that was made in connection with it, were designed to create doubt in the minds of people as to the sincerity of hon. members who have taken a stand on this matter.
My stand, sir, is perfectly clear. I spoke at the resolution stage. My vote is already

on the record on second reading of this bill. I am opposed to this measure, and I am opposed to it as a member of this house expressing my best judgment as to what is best for this parliament and for the country as a whole; and I will not have anyone imputing motives on an occasion of this kind, trying to create any doubt in anyone's mind as to the sincerity of hon. members. I have too much respect for hon. members who are on both sides of this question to accept this kind of childish motion.
I will go this far with the hon. member for Macleod. He apparently wants to throw out a challenge. I am willing to take up the glove, and I will give him this deal. If he is willing to accept his increase for which he voted in Social Credit scrip I will be glad to take nothing at all.

The hon. members to. my left with whose doctrine I have never been in full agreement have now put forward this amendment. I was rather impressed with the leader of the party to our immediate left and his right bower who sits to his left, who are diametrically opposed to each other on this issue. It shows they must be sincere. The hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway, to whom I rarely if ever pay a compliment- and I hesitate to do it now unless it is wrapped up in a brick or something-has evidenced a certain sincerity. He is a man who started from the grass roots of endeavour in this country, and anyone who listened to his speech-and I have listened to him on
Senate and House of Commons other occasions-must admit that he has shown integrity of purpose and sincerity in his expression of opinion no matter whether you agree with him or not. I must say that he spoke most sincerely, and he needs the money as badly as any of us.
The hon. member for Macleod, one of those great social reformers down to the far left, suggests tonight that we should have two social classes in this parliament. He would go further than my friends to my immediate left would venture. I do not think they will ever go that far. He would go so far as the whole communist doctrine which would say that we shall serve according to our ability and accept according to our needs. Of all the ridiculous doctrines I have ever heard this is the most ridiculous.
I do not mind telling you that I have heard people on the sideroads say that in some respects the Social Crediters have some of the sound virtues of the Conservative party. When I listened to them tonight I could realize why the Speaker sat them so far to the left. They are even farther to the left than the C.C.F. when they would suggest two social classes in this parliament. Why, these same gentlemen, Mr. Chairman, have pleaded almost with crocodile tears in this house that we must not have a means test for the old age pensions. They said, "Oh, don't make these old age pensioners ever have to take a means test." I am not so sure, speaking personally and independently of my party, that that was too sound. I am not quite that old yet. On numerous occasions I had to pass a means test, when I went to my banker in order to keep my children in university while I was serving in this house. That means test embarrassed me, as between my banker and myself. I always looked over my shoulder to see that some Grit financier was not laughing at me. My hon. friends to my left and the hon. member for Macleod would suggest that we have a means test for members of parliament.

I will go there for nothing because I will meet a lot of friends, and I might get my own out of it some way or another". That is no reflection on any hon. member here from the Prime Minister down, and including his predecessors in this parliament; for during the many years I have been here I have sat in clubs, I have sat in Conservative circles and in other gatherings and

Senate and House of Commons have told people that those who believe that men come to this parliament to make money are wrong.
The Liberals have been in power during the greatest time of my regime here, and that is a compliment to them. But it is only human nature. I would not need the fingers of one hand nor even two fingers of one hand, to count the number of men who have come to the Canadian parliament in the last quarter of a century that I personally know have benefited by crooked misrepresentation or taking advantage of contracts. I say that advisedly. I know something of the regime, though I do not know it all; and I know something of how campaign funds come along. They seem to have flowed in a little more rapidly lately. I cannot keep track of them, especially when I think of my younger and more tolerant years. The present government benefited or were able to get campaign funds such as I never dreamed of, maybe because they are able to do it better than I could.

I am not going to enlarge upon it, except to say that as members of Her Majesty's loyal opposition we have tried to show that this matter should have been given more study. We have not opposed the principle of increased indemnities as such in order to encourage better men than you or I to enter politics and come to this house. We have not opposed that. We have not opposed the general principle; we believe there should have been an increase.
Some of those who heckle the most should understand that as far as the taxpayers of Canada are concerned they do not measure their ability by their anxiety to have a larger indemnity. Some of those who have seldom risen in the house are the most vociferous about getting a larger indemnity. They are probably the members who never made as much money at anything else in their life.
I shall conclude, Mr. Speaker, by saying that our motive should not be ill-considered. Our motives have been sound. We have pressed for a study of this problem. I will say in all fairness that this has been a difficult problem for the Prime Minister. It has been equally difficult for the Leader of the Opposition, and a difficult problem for every member of the house because it involves ourselves. We are now working on our own salaries. In doing so we give the lead to every civil servant in Canada; we give the lead to every employee in Canada; and we are giving the lead to every labour union in Canada. Even though we say that we
Senate and House of Commons should have lower costs of production we are increasing our indemnities 100 per cent.
If the majority overrules our efforts to have a more thorough study of this proposal, will the people agree and will the taxpayer agree that we are entitled to at least as much salary as those of you who have been civil servants? I might also say to the hon. member for Macleod that with this increase in indemnity we do not wish to start a form of social distinction in this house, and I would say to him again that the people of my riding believe I am worth as much as he is.

Before you proceed with
clause 3, or perhaps it might be regarded as on clause 3, I should like to put a question to the Prime Minister. You will see in a moment, Mr. Chairman, why I raise the point at this juncture. Clause 3 of the bill provides for the repeal of sections 39 and 40 of the act. The desirability of repealing those sections is obvious in view of the change to an annual basis.
My question at this point is this. In between section 35 of the Senate and House of Commons Act which we have amended by a previous clause of this bill, and section 39 of the Senate and House of Commons Act which it is now proposed should be repealed, there is section 36 of the Senate and House of Commons Act. I made a few remarks on this question last night and I do not intend to develop them at any length at this point. However, I should like to add just one or two facts to what I stated last night. The other

Senate and House of Commons
day the Prime Minister pointed out that the question of the total payment made to members has been before parliament on a number of occasions. There was the statute in 1867 which set the first figure. It has been changed five times since then. This will be the sixth occasion on which the total amount paid to members of parliament has been changed since it was first established in 1867.
My point is this, Mr. Chairman. On every one of those previous occasions when a change has been made in the total amount of money paid to members of parliament, a corresponding change has been made in the amount that a member might lose per day for absence in excess of whatever period of time was considered to be permissible. For a long time now that allowable period of absence has been 15 days per session, but it has been the law of the land right back to 1867 that absence in excess of what is permitted should result in the loss of some portion of the member's total pay. Originally the deduction was only $5 per day. Since then it has been raised to $8, then to $10, $15, $25 and in 1945 to $37.50.
The question I now put to the Prime Minister is, I think, an obvious one. Why is it that on this occasion, when another change is being made in the amount of the indemnity, that corresponding change which has been made every other time seems to have been omitted?

It is 50 per cent of whatever is deducted under section 36. Serious consideration was given to whether we should recommend that there be any stricter measures in order to ensure perhaps closer attendance in the house. There were many who were of the opinion that this was something that was the concern of the electors of each individual member; that when the member was away attending some function in his constituency while parliament was sitting, his electors knew that he was not present in parliament; and that there were many
occasions when they felt that he was performing, as they wished him to perform them, his duties as their representative by attending functions in his constituency. Nevertheless, the principle is that there is a deduction to be made; and in fact over the years there have been many occasions-I think almost every year since I have been here-when in the supplementary estimates there was a special vote to enable payment to be made to members who, for one reason or another, had exceeded the number of absences provided for in the statute.
The conclusion we came to was that we would have to be much more careful now in recommending supplementary estimates to make up for the deductions that would be made for absences from the house. I have no personal views as to whether the figure should remain at $25. If we want to have it just about in the same proportion as it was before, I think something like $40 instead of $25 in section 36 would make it $60 over-all, and that figure would be just about in the same proportion as that in existence since confederation.
I am not going to suggest an amendment. As a matter of fact I may not do so as it is my own bill. It would not be in order for me to submit an amendment to my own bill, even if I felt so inclined. But if any hon. member feels that section 36 should be amended to provide some increase in the penalty by way of deduction for being out of the house more than 15 days during the session, I think this is the time and place when it would be appropriate to submit that kind of amendment.
I shall add also that there is in section 41 of the Senate and House of Commons Act a provision whereby the Senate or the House of Commons may respectively make regulations from time to time, by rule or by order, rendering more stringent upon its own members the provisions of this act that relate to the attendance of members or to deductions to be made from the sessional allowance. The question was raised as to whether or not there should be some daily record of the attendance of members. We felt that was not something that should be dealt with by statute. In the other place, I presume it must be by some rule made under section 41, a record is kept in Votes and Proceedings of the daily attendance of members.
There is a committee of members sitting with His Honour the Speaker at the present time dealing with the rules of the house. It is rather difficult to say that one should determine for the electors of a constituency how they want their representative to represent them. The matter could be dealt with by a
1718	HOUSE OF
Senate and House of Commons rule of the house providing some method whereby a record of attendance would be kept; that is something the house itself should consider. However, if the rate of deduction is to be more than $37.50, there will have to be an amendment to section 36. I believe the figure that would bring the deduction into proportion with the increase in the indemnity might be $40 instead of $25, because that would in reality amount to a deduction of $60.

I wish to thank the Prime Minister for the manner in which he has discussed this matter, Mr. Chairman, and to say at once that I agree with him that making a final decision about what to do in this matter in committee of the whole does present some difficulties. May I say at this time, too, that our thinking is perhaps closer together than he realized. When I was suggesting a certain figure last night, namely $60 or $62.50, I was suggesting that in relation to the present $37.50. In other words I was proposing an over-all figure. I indicated that in my view perhaps the amount might be higher, but I put that forward as being proportionate to the deduction now made.
What the Prime Minister now suggests, namely that the present figure of $25 as a deduction from the indemnity might be raised to $40, has the actual effect of making the loss per day $60 because the other section increases that deduction by 50 per cent with respect to the expense allowance. I did not draft an amendment with respect to this matter. One of my friends in the party to the right tells me he attempted to draft one, but certain difficulties presented themselves to his mind as well. It does seem to me that this bill should not be rushed through, certainly not through its final stage, without some further thought being given to this matter. Since the subject has been raised, it may be that some comments will be made which might give a lead to the government, on the basis of which a section might be put into the bill before it is given third reading.
I agree with the suggestion made by the Prime Minister that the committee on rules might well take certain steps under the provisions of section 41 of the Senate and House of Commons Act to recommend more stringent regulations respecting attendance, and also with respect to keeping a record of attendance. But as the Prime Minister has just said, and I think I am quoting him correctly, if anything were to be done concerning the deductions from our pay in terms of dollars, that would have to be by way of amendment to section 36 of the Senate and


House of Commons Act. It has been suggested to me that an amendment of that kind could come later, but our experience around here generally is that once a bill, particularly a bill that is such a problem as this one, has been disposed of, the government does not like to reopen it to make other amendments.
I am sure the Prime Minister will not be asking for third reading of this bill tonight, even if we get through the committee stage. After all, it received second reading today and it cannot have third reading today without unanimous consent. I would hope that he and his colleagues would consider the desirability of proposing another clause for Bill No. 171 which would go in between clause 2 and clause 3, and would have the effect of amending section 36 of the Senate and House of Commons Act. I want to say quite frankly that I believe the figure should be a lot higher than the one I suggested last night. I think it should be higher than the figure proposed by the Prime Minister, but at least I would go as far as he is going and support that figure as better than the one that now exists.
The reason I would suggest the figure being higher is that even if the total loss to a member for days absent in excess 'of 15 is put at $60, it is still possible for a member to be absent from the house-let us take the extreme case which I trust does not happen-a full session and receive a pretty fair remuneration. The average length of a session is around 115 sitting days. A member could be absent the whole of the 115 days, and since 15 of them are allowable he would suffer a deduction for only 100 days. Assuming he reports all those days as being absent, if the loss is $60 a day, 100 times $60 is $6,000, which would mean he could still draw $4,000 for not having attended a session at all during that year. Now, my case is hypothetical, and it is based on that number of sitting days per year. If the number of sitting days is more or less the result will vary, but I do not think the hypothesis is too far from reality.
I suggest that example merely to point out that we are not being unreasonable in suggesting a loss of $60 per day. This would be the result if the Prime Minister introduced an amendment to section 36 so that the $25 would read $40, for an additional $20 would be deducted under the later section. I am one of those who feel that other changes should be made in respect to attendance, but I am inclined to think the Prime Minister's suggestion is a good one. I believe that sort of thing can be best dealt

with in the committee on procedure. Since I am a member of that committee, I shall have the opportunity to state my views there. I do urge the Prime Minister to consider the possibility of introducing a clause amending section 36, along the lines we have discussed just now, before this bill receives third reading.

I should like to say a word
or two on this subject. I agree in general with the approach indicated by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre. The amount of the increase in indemnity is now a fact, so there is no point in discussing that further. It is a substantial sum that members are now to receive, and I urge upon the Prime Minister and the members of the house generally that in so far as we can do it we should ensure that the opportunities for the receipt of that amount of money by a member are made above reproach. In so far as we can do it, and only in so far as we can do it, we should eliminate the possibility that unpleasant incidents will arise where the attention of the public is drawn to the fact that so-and-so has received his remuneration as a member when, in fact, he did not attend in the House of Commons for the length of time for which, in accordance with the spirit of the act, he should have attended if he were to receive that amount of money.
I think there are ways in which that result can be accomplished. I do think we should give consideration to the question of how we can better ensure attendance in Ottawa and at the sittings of the house, in order to qualify members so they may receive indemnities. I do not mean that they have to be sitting in the chamber all day; but they would have to be here in Ottawa, where they are attending their parliamentary duties.
At the same time, while I agree that the matter can be taken care of in section 41, to which the Prime Minister referred, through having that section reviewed by the committee on procedure, I do not think it is inconsistent with what I have said with respect to tightening up the regulations when I make the suggestion that if we are going to tighten them we will have to make sure that they are reasonable, and that they conform to the obligations of a member to go back to his constituency occasionally.
I would suggest that the present allowable absence of 15 days, which is statutory, and therefore cannot be reviewed by the rules committee, should therefore be reviewed here. I believe it should be reviewed because it is a provision which has been in existence for a long time. I do not know how long, but certainly since 1927. I would assume that it was there for some considerable number of years before that.
Senate and House of Commons
I think I am correct when I say that the length of sessions has very considerably increased since the 15 days was stipulated. So my approach to the subject is to suggest that possibly the allowable number of days of absence should be increased to perhaps three weeks or 21 days, or whatever length of time might be felt reasonable, and that the requirements for the attendance of members on other days should be tightened up by the rules committee. But inasmuch as the allowable days of absence is statutory I would like the Prime Minister to consult with his colleagues to see whether it is reasonable to suggest that under the circumstances that length of time might be increased, particularly if we are going to take the other step-as I hope we will-of tightening up the regulation regarding attendance in Ottawa.

If I may meet part way the wishes of hon. members, who are honouring me by shouting my first name, I would say that I do not propose moving any amendment to clause 4, but I do urge the House of Commons to vote against it.
My main reason for urging opposition to clause 4 has to do with what is provided in that part of it that amends section 43 of the Senate and House of Commons Act. I had thought of confining my opposition to this clause to that part that amends section 43 of the Senate and House of Commons Act; but in view of the remarks that have been made throughout the course of this debate by the Leader of the Opposition I am sure he will agree with me that one should not distinguish, but that one should oppose the whole clause.
After all, I am sure the present Leader of the Opposition does not want his annual allowance raised to $15,000 until the matter has been referred to a royal commission. However, it was not that part of the clause that bothered me most. I am concerned about the increases proposed for the leader of the government and the leader of the opposition in the Senate. Hon. members who have been here for a number of years will recall that back in 1947, when it was first proposed that there be any salaries at all for the two leaders in the other house-that is, salaries in addition to their indemnities as senators-we opposed that action.
I had occasion within the last day or so to look back over the debates of that occasion, debates which waxed rather warm. As a matter of fact the rules of the other house were broken a bit in that when the bill got over there they had something to say about some of the things that had been said in this house. Nevertheless we made it clear at that time, as I make it clear again now, that this is not a matter which relates to the particular persons who happen at any time to be occupying those positions. We in this group feel, however, that, our opposition to the move in 1947 having been overruled, the salaries provided for the two leaders in the other place, in addition to their indemnities, are quite adequate.
The section with regard to the indemnities for senators and members of the House of Commons has now been passed, and that amount will be $10,000 a year. The salary for the leader of the government in the other place, provided he is not in receipt of a salary under the Salaries Act-which happens to be the case at this time-is $7,000 a year at the present time. That is, if we defeat


this clause the total emolument for the leader of the government in the Senate, provided that is all he is, would be $10,000 indemnity as a senator, plus $7,000 salary. The leader of the opposition in the Senate at the present time would get $10,000 indemnity and $4,000 salary.
We do not think it is necessary to increase the salary of the leader of the government in the other place from $7,000 to $10,000, making his total emolument $20,000; neither do we think it is necessary to increase the salary of the leader of the opposition in the other place from $4,000 to $6,000, thus making his total emolument $16,000. I repeat that this has no relationship to the present or any future incumbents of those positions. It has no relation to their political connections. It has no relation to the number of followers they may have. It is just as a matter of principle; and in the light of the amount of work that has to be done, bearing in mind also that persons who occupy those positions receive something more than money-they have the dignity and the honour that goes with them- I think the emoluments they will receive under the $10,000 indemnity, plus the salaries they are now receiving, are adequate. A great many people in this country will feel that they are too much.
In any case, the holders of these positions are getting an increase of $4,000 a year by virtue of the increased indemnity. I feel, particularly because of what is involved in the change in section 43 of the Senate and House of Commons Act by virtue of clause 4 of this bill, that this house should now turn down clause 4.

I do not believe there is anything before us to indicate how these figures are arrived at. We are not dealing with the particular amount payable to any individual. The amounts are payable to those who occupy positions in parliament and should be regarded in that light. I oppose this section as I have opposed the other sections of this bill.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I think it would be the wish of most hon. members, if not

all, to dispose of the committee stage, if possible, tonight. In view of the discussion that has just occurred between the Prime Minister and hon. members opposite who spoke of certain suggested amendments, I have at the request of the Prime Minister a suggestion to make. It is in the form of a suggestion, sir, and reads:
That clauses 3 and 4 of the bill be renumbered 4 and 5 respectively; that there be inserted then as clause 3 the following:
Section 36 is amended by substituting the word "forty" for the word "twenty-five" as it appears in the first line thereof and that the word "twenty-one" be substituted for the word "fifteen" as it appears in the other parts of the section.
-and that these amendments be properly drafted by the law clerk of the house. I should add and by way of explanation, Mr. Chairman, that it is not the intention of the government to call the bill for third reading until hon. members have had an opportunity to see the printed bill in its new form.
